stem: Which of the following ions has the greatest concentration gradient across a typical cell membrane at rest? (select one correct response)

a.why: Calcium: about 1.2 millimolar outside vs about 100 nanomolar in cytosol, roughly a 10,000-fold gradient. Sodium, potassium and chloride gradients are only about 10- to 30-fold.

stem: The membrane potential for a nerve is determined to be +30 mV (cytosol is positive). Which of the following relationships regarding membrane permeabilities is likely true? (select one correct response)

a.why: A +30 millivolt potential sits near the sodium equilibrium potential, so sodium permeability must dominate; potassium permeability must be lowest or it would pull the potential negative.

stem: Which of the following toxins is used clinically to inhibit nerve function by interacting with either T-SNAREs or V-SNAREs to block the release of acetylcholine from vesicles at nerve terminals? (select one correct response)

a.why: Botulinum toxins are proteases that cleave SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin, SNAP-25, syntaxin), blocking acetylcholine vesicle fusion. Alpha-bungarotoxin blocks the postsynaptic nicotinic receptor instead; tetrodotoxin blocks sodium channels.

stem: In which G-protein coupled pathway does the G-protein α subunit reduce the activity of an enzyme by direct interaction? (select one correct response)

a.why: The inhibitory G-protein alpha subunit (G alpha i) binds adenylyl cyclase directly and lowers cyclic AMP production. G alpha s stimulates it; G alpha q activates phospholipase C.

stem: Which of the following voltage-sensitive channels is expressed in the heart and is affected by a variety of drugs, such as cisapride and sotalol, to cause arrhythmias that can lead to sudden cardiac death? (select one correct response)

a.why: hERG (human ether-a-go-go related gene, Kv11.1) carries the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current in heart; cisapride and sotalol block it, prolonging the QT interval and risking fatal arrhythmia.

stem: Which of the following statements is true with respect to voltage-sensitive Na⁺ channels (Na_(v)), voltage-sensitive K⁺ channels (K_(v)) and voltage-sensitive Ca²⁺ channels (Ca_(v))? (Select ALL answers that are correct)
opts: Each can be blocked by a naturally-occurring toxin (e.g., tetrodotoxin, charybdotoxin, conotoxin, etc.)
Each channel is highly selective for the cation from which it derives its name.
Each type of channel has an inactivation mechanism that limits the duration in the activated or conductive state.
Four ‘P loops’ form the selectivity filter of the ion channel of each.
TM4 (or S4) is the voltage sensor for channel activation. There are four voltage-sensing segments in each channel.

a.why: All five hold for the course model: each has toxins, is selective, has an inactivated state (Schultz's Kv diagram shows one), four P loops form the filter, and four S4 segments sense voltage.
a.cite: outside course materials + exam state diagrams
a.flag: Many Kv channels (delayed rectifiers) lack fast inactivation, so (c) could be keyed false; Schultz's own Kv diagram shows an inactivated state, so all five chosen.

stem: Your patient suffers severe trauma to the right half of the spinal cord at T6/T7 (right spinal hemisection at thoracic vertebrae 6 and 7). Which of the following statements is true? (select one correct response)
opts: The patient will exhibit reduced sensation to somatic touch in the right hind limb and reduced sensation to temperature and pain in the left hind limb.
The patient will exhibit reduced sensation to somatic touch in the left hind limb and reduced sensation to temperature and pain in the right hind limb.
The patient will exhibit enhanced sensation to somatic touch in the right hind limb and enhanced sensation to temperature and pain in the left hind limb.
The patient will exhibit enhanced sensation to somatic touch in the left hind limb and enhanced sensation to temperature and pain in the right hind limb.
The patient will exhibit reduced sensation to somatic touch and reduced sensation to temperature and pain in both hind limbs.

a.why: Hemisection (Brown-Sequard): dorsal columns (touch) travel uncrossed, so touch is lost on the same (right) side; spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature) crosses at entry, so loss is on the opposite (left) side.

stem: Shown to the right are two cells that communicate via gap junctions. Which of the following could act as a signaling molecule to the target cell in this system? (select one correct response)

a.why: Inositol trisphosphate is small (under 1,000 daltons) and passes through gap junctions. Connexin is the channel protein itself; guanylyl cyclase and SOS are proteins; CD11 is a membrane integrin.

stem: How many connexin molecules are required to form one connexon? (select one correct response)
opts: A substantial number, usually numbering well into the hundreds.

a.why: One connexon (hemichannel) is a hexamer of 6 connexins. Two connexons, one from each cell, dock to make one gap junction channel (12 connexins total). Trap: 12 answers a different question.

stem: Which of the states are non-conductive (i.e., ions cannot flow through these channels in these states)? (select three correct responses)
ctx: Shown below are state diagrams for voltage-sensitive Na⁺ channels (Na_(v)) and for voltage-sensitive K⁺ channels (K_(v)). Use these images to answer questions 10-13. [] []

a.why: Non-conductive: voltage-gated potassium channel resting, sodium channel resting (closed gate) and sodium channel inactivated (inactivation gate plugs the pore). Both 'activated' states are open and conduct.

stem: Which channel states are associated with the absolute refractory period? (select two correct responses)

a.why: Absolute refractory period: sodium channels are already open (activated) or inactivated, so no stimulus can trigger a new action potential.

stem: Which channel state is associated with the relative refractory period? (select one correct response)

a.why: Relative refractory period: potassium channels are still activated (open), hyperpolarizing the cell, so a larger-than-normal stimulus is needed while sodium channels recover from inactivation.
a.flag: Some texts emphasize sodium channels returning to resting as the relative refractory feature; the open potassium channel is the best single choice here.

stem: What event or condition causes activation (i.e., the transition from ‘resting state’ to ‘activated state’) for both Na_(v) and K_(v) channels? (select one correct response)
opts: Time and inactivation mechanism (hinged lid or ball and chain)

a.why: Membrane depolarization moves the S4 voltage sensors outward, opening (activating) both voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels. Hyperpolarization and time return them to rest.

stem: Which of the following is a signaling or receptor molecule that is involved with contact-dependent signaling following ischemia and reperfusion? (select one correct response)

a.why: After ischemia-reperfusion, white blood cells adhere to endothelium via selectins then integrins (CD11 alpha, CD18 beta) binding intercellular adhesion molecules: contact-dependent signaling. Histamine is paracrine.

stem: Which signaling molecule in the following list has the highest octanol:water partition coefficient? (select one correct response)

a.why: Cholesterol is the most lipid-soluble (log P around 7-8). Aldosterone is about 1.1; acetylcholine, histamine and oxytocin are water-soluble (negative log P).
a.cite: LC21 transcript (log P examples) + outside for cholesterol value

stem: Both nitric oxide (NO) and atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) cause vasodilation that results from the relaxation of vascular smooth muscle. What common cytosolic second messenger is produced in vascular smooth muscle following exposure to these agonists? (select one correct response)

a.why: Both activate guanylyl cyclase (soluble for nitric oxide, membrane receptor for atrial natriuretic peptide), producing cyclic GMP. Trap: guanylyl cyclase is the enzyme, not the second messenger.
a.cite: LC21 transcript (nitric oxide to guanylyl cyclase)

stem: In the mitogen activated protein kinase second messenger pathway (MAPK), what protein binds to RAS and acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor to promote GTP binding? (select one correct response)
opts: Mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase (MAP KKK)

a.why: Son of Sevenless is the guanine nucleotide exchange factor recruited by Grb2 to RAS, swapping GDP for GTP. Insulin receptor substrate 1 is an adaptor; MAP kinase kinase kinase (Raf) is downstream of RAS.

stem: Which of the following is a cholesterol derivative that interacts with and binds to an intracellular steroid hormone receptor? (select one correct response)

a.why: Testosterone is a steroid made from cholesterol and binds the intracellular androgen receptor. Retinoic acid and thyroxine are not cholesterol derivatives; cholesterol itself is not a hormone receptor ligand.
a.flag: Vitamin D3 is also cholesterol-derived, but must be converted to calcitriol before binding the vitamin D receptor; testosterone is the cleaner answer.

stem: In circulation, which of the following signaling molecules associates with both transthyretin and thyroxine binding globulin? (select one correct response)

a.why: Thyroxine is carried by thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin and albumin. Cortisol uses corticosteroid-binding globulin; estradiol uses sex hormone-binding globulin; thyroid stimulating hormone and thyrotropin releasing hormone are water-soluble.

stem: In an epithelial cell that expresses high amounts of active 11-β hydroxy steroid dehydrogenase 2 (11-β HSD2), what naturally-occurring signaling molecule enhances the expression of SGK1, ENaC, and ROMK? (select one correct response)

a.why: 11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 2 converts cortisol to inactive cortisone, protecting the cell so aldosterone can drive serum and glucocorticoid kinase 1, epithelial sodium channel and renal outer medullary potassium channel expression.
a.flag: 11-beta HSD2 role is outside LC21 transcript coverage.

stem: In reference to question 20, what receptor is targeted selectively by the naturally occurring agonist? (select one correct response)

a.why: Aldosterone acts on the mineralocorticoid receptor, which moves to the nucleus and drives transcription. Glucocorticoid receptor binds cortisol; cortisol is kept off the mineralocorticoid receptor by 11-beta HSD2.

stem: Chili peppers (capsaicin) are used both in chemesthesis (to enhance flavor sensation) and as a topical rub (e.g., Icy-Hot). Which receptor type or channel type is targeted by capsaicin? (Select one correct response)

a.why: Capsaicin activates transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), a heat/pain-sensing cation channel. Acid-sensing ion channels respond to protons; Piezo channels to mechanical stretch.

stem: Which amino acids in a growth factor receptor are phosphorylated in response to ligand binding? (select one correct response)

a.why: Growth factor receptors are receptor tyrosine kinases: ligand binding causes dimerization and autophosphorylation of tyrosine residues, creating docking sites (SH2 domains) for downstream proteins.

stem: After hormone binding, which portion of the steroid hormone receptor must be exposed to allow for receptor specificity to its binding site? (select one correct response)

a.why: Hormone binding releases chaperones (heat shock proteins) and exposes the DNA binding domain (zinc fingers), which recognizes specific hormone response elements on DNA.

stem: In the thyroid hormone pathway, which extracellular signaling molecule provides negative feedback to reduce hormone release from the anterior pituitary? (select one correct response)

a.why: Circulating thyroxine (converted to tri-iodothyronine in pituitary) feeds back to suppress thyroid stimulating hormone release. Thyroid stimulating hormone is the pituitary output; reverse tri-iodothyronine is inactive; deiodinase is an enzyme.

stem: Which of the following enzymes is effectively a ‘timer’ that determines the duration that a cell remains in the ‘activated’ state following insulin (or growth factor) binding to its cognate receptor? (select one correct response)

a.why: RAS is a small G-protein; its intrinsic GTPase hydrolyzes GTP to GDP, switching it off, so the GTP-hydrolysis rate sets how long the cell stays activated. Calcium is an ion, not an enzyme.

stem: Caffeine is a broad-spectrum phosphodiesterase inhibitor (i.e., the enzyme that breaks down cyclic nucleotides). Which pathway will have its effect enhanced or prolonged in the presence of caffeine? (select one correct response)
opts: In heart, Norepinephrine –> β1 receptor -> G_(s) -> …
In heart, Acetylcholine –> M2 receptor -> G_(i) -> …
In vascular muscle, Norepinephrine –> α1 receptor –> G_(q) –> IP₃ -> CaM -> …
In vascular muscle, Norepinephrine –> α1 receptor –> G_(q) –> DAG -> PKC -> …
In vascular muscle, Histamine –> H1 receptor –> G_(q) –> IP₃ -> NOS -> …

a.why: Caffeine blocks phosphodiesterase, so cyclic AMP persists: the beta-1, stimulatory G-protein (Gs), adenylyl cyclase, cyclic AMP pathway is prolonged. M2/Gi lowers cyclic AMP, so it is opposed.
a.flag: 2024 version of this question asks for two and option e (histamine to nitric oxide to cyclic GMP) is also prolonged; if single-answer keyed, a is the best pick.

stem: The incorporation of cytosolic vesicles into the cell membrane requires signals for vesicle trafficking and exocytosis. Ca²⁺ is often a second messenger in these pathways and a local increase of ten-fold to one hundred-fold in cytosolic Ca²⁺ concentration can be required for exocytosis. At rest, what is reputed to be a typical cytosolic Ca²⁺ concentration? (indicate all that are correct)

a.why: Resting cytosolic calcium is about 100 nanomolar = 0.1 micromolar = 10^-7 molar = 10^-4 millimolar. 10^-4 molar is 100 micromolar, 1,000 times too high.

stem: Biogenic amines and amino acid neurotransmitters are removed from synapses by four families of cotransporters. All of the transporters move neurotransmitters against their concentration gradients. What energy source is used to directly support the transport activity? (Select one correct response)

a.why: Neurotransmitter reuptake transporters are secondary active symporters driven directly by the sodium electrochemical gradient (often with chloride). ATP powers the sodium-potassium pump only indirectly.

stem: Shown to the right is a prototypical action potential with five labeled locations. The action potential was initiated by exposure to glutamate. Below is a GHK equation with numbers shown for the permeabilities to selected ions just below the associated conductances or concentration gradients. What point in the action potential (A, B, C, D, E) is best described by the equation with the indicated permeabilities? (Select one correct response: an arrow can be added to the action potential to indicate the point depicted by the equation) P_(K)=1 P_(Na)=0.03 P_(Cl)=0.1 P_(GlutR)=0.5 P_(Cl-R)=0.0 P_(Nav)=0.0 P_(Kv)=0.0 (Point choices: A, B, C, D, E on the action potential image.)

a.why: Glutamate receptor permeability is on but voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels are still closed: the glutamate-driven depolarization rising toward threshold, just before the upstroke, is point B.

stem: Shown below is an image that includes two presynaptic nerve terminals, a postsynaptic cell and an astrocyte. Some structures are depicted, but much of the labeling has been removed. Some clues regarding the neurotransmitters, receptors and transporters are included. Label components of the cells as completely as possible. Draw and label additional components, ion gradients, drugs or toxins that enhance the image. In five sentences or less, describe the synapse and and the effects of the neurotransmitters, drugs or toxins.

a.why: Left terminal is glycinergic: serine is converted to glycine, vesicular inhibitory amino acid transporter fills vesicles, GlyT2 (3 sodium, 1 chloride) recycles glycine. Right terminal releases glutamate; excitatory amino acid transporters clear it. Astrocyte GlyT1 (2 sodium, 1 chloride) takes up glycine. Postsynaptic glycine receptors (chloride channels, anchored by gephyrin) hyperpolarize because K-Cl cotransporter 2 keeps chloride low; AMPA receptors depolarize; NMDA receptors need glutamate plus glycine co-agonist. Strychnine blocks glycine receptors; tetanus toxin blocks glycine release causing spasticity.

stem: Which of the following is an inhibitor of 5 alpha reductase that can be used to treat prostatic hyperplasia and/or male pattern baldness? (select one correct response)

a.why: Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha reductase, blocking testosterone to dihydrotestosterone conversion, shrinking the prostate and slowing hair loss. Aromatase converts testosterone to estradiol; 11-beta HSD inactivates cortisol.

stem: Which of the following is a physiological agonist for a ‘steroid hormone receptor’ but is not a steroid or a cholesterol derivative? (select one correct response)

a.why: Tri-iodothyronine is an iodinated tyrosine derivative, not a steroid, yet binds the nuclear thyroid hormone receptor of the steroid receptor superfamily. Estradiol and progesterone are steroids; ANP and histamine use surface receptors.
a.cite: LC21 transcript (thyroid hormone grouped with intracellular receptors)

stem: What molecule is hydrolyzed by the alpha subunits of G-proteins? (select one correct response)

a.why: G-protein alpha subunits are GTPases: they hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP, which ends their active state.

stem: Which type of intercellular signaling is associated with selectins, integrins and glycoprotein adhesion molecules? (select one correct response)

a.why: Selectins, integrins and adhesion molecules require physical cell-to-cell contact: contact-dependent signaling (e.g., white blood cell adhesion to endothelium).

stem: Which of the following limits the effectiveness or timely usefulness of paracrine signaling? (select one correct response)
opts: Diffusion distance to the target cell

a.why: Paracrine signaling depends on diffusion, so it only works over short distances; diffusion time grows with distance squared.

stem: The incorporation of cytosolic vesicles into the cell membrane requires signals for vesicle trafficking and exocytosis. Ca²⁺ is often a second messenger in these pathways and a local increase of ten-fold to one hundred-fold in cytosolic Ca²⁺ concentration can be required for exocytosis. At rest, what is reported to be a typical cytosolic Ca²⁺ concentration? (select all that are correct)

a.why: 100 nanomolar = 10^-7 molar = 10^-4 millimolar. Trap: 10^-4 micromolar is only 0.1 nanomolar (1,000 times too low); 100 micromolar is 1,000 times too high.

stem: Based upon their molecular masses, which of the following will likely pass through a gap junction? (select two correct responses)

a.why: Gap junctions pass molecules under about 1,000 daltons: asparagine (about 132) and cyclic GMP (about 345). Insulin, epithelial sodium channel and phospholipase C are proteins, far too large.

stem: Glutamate is an amino acid used by the body as a signaling molecule (neurotransmitter). Based on your knowledge of glutamate and of receptors, which of the following statements is true regarding glutamate and/or its receptor? (select one correct response)
opts: Glutamate has a large positive LogP (high octanol:water partition coefficient)
Glutamate is carried through circulation bound to an excitatory amino acid binding globulin (EEABG)
Glutamate receptors are in the cell membrane (like histamine receptors)
Glutamate receptor are in the cytosol (like steroid hormone receptors)

a.why: Glutamate is charged and water-soluble (negative log P), cannot cross membranes, so its receptors sit in the cell membrane, like histamine receptors. No carrier protein is needed.
a.cite: LC21 transcript (log P and receptor location)

stem: After hormone binding, which portion of the steroid hormone receptor must be exposed to allow for receptor specificity to its binding site? (select one correct response)

a.why: After hormone binding, the DNA binding domain (zinc fingers) is exposed so the receptor recognizes specific hormone response elements on DNA.

stem: Thyroid stimulating hormone causes an increase in the concentration of cAMP in thyroid cells. How many transmembrane segments are present in the receptor and which G-protein is coupled with this receptor? (select one correct response)

a.why: The thyroid stimulating hormone receptor is a G-protein coupled receptor (7 transmembrane segments) using the stimulatory G-protein (Gs) to activate adenylyl cyclase and raise cyclic AMP. Gq would raise calcium instead.

stem: Prazosin interacts with and binds to the same location as norepinephrine on the alpha-1 adrenergic receptor, but causes no change in G-protein activity or in phospholipase C activity. Which of the following terms best describes prazosin? (select one correct response)

a.why: Prazosin binds the receptor's agonist site but produces no response, blocking norepinephrine: an antagonist. It is technically a ligand too, but 'antagonist' is the most specific description.

stem: In the thyroid hormone pathway, which extracellular signaling molecule provides negative feedback to reduce hormone release from the anterior pituitary? (select one correct response)

a.why: Thyroxine and tri-iodothyronine feed back on pituitary (and hypothalamus) to cut thyroid stimulating hormone release. Thyroid stimulating hormone is the output being suppressed; deiodinase is an enzyme.

stem: Which of the following enzymes is effectively a ‘timer’ that determines the duration that a cell remains in the ‘activated’ state following insulin (or growth factor) binding to its cognate receptor? (select one correct response)

a.why: RAS hydrolyzes its own GTP; the rate of that GTPase activity sets how long the growth factor/insulin signal stays on. Gs and Gq belong to G-protein coupled pathways; calcium is not an enzyme.

stem: Caffeine is a broad-spectrum phosphodiesterase inhibitor (i.e., the enzyme that breaks down cyclic nucleotides). Which pathways will have their effects enhanced or prolonged in the presence of caffeine? (select two correct responses)
opts: In heart, Norepinephrine –> β1 receptor -> G_(s) -> …
In heart, Acetylcholine –> M2 receptor -> G_(i) -> …
In vascular muscle, Norepinephrine –> α1 receptor –> G_(q) –> IP₃ -> CaM -> …
In vascular muscle, Norepinephrine –> α1 receptor –> G_(q) –> DAG -> PKC -> …
In vascular muscle, Histamine –> H1 receptor –> G_(q) –> IP₃ -> NOS -> …

a.why: Phosphodiesterase inhibition prolongs cyclic nucleotides: beta-1/Gs raises cyclic AMP (a); histamine H1 to nitric oxide synthase leads to nitric oxide raising cyclic GMP in smooth muscle (e). Gi lowers cyclic AMP; Gq IP3/DAG branches use none.

stem: Which of the following enzymes is required to reduce the cytosolic concentration of a small molecule second messenger in the Gq (NO) pathway? (select one correct response)

a.why: In the histamine/Gq pathway that makes nitric oxide, the small-molecule second messenger driving nitric oxide synthase is calcium; endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase pumps it back out of the cytosol.
a.flag: 'DAG phosphatase' is not the real DAG-clearing enzyme (DAG kinase or lipase is).

stem: Which three of the following signaling molecules are lipid soluble and have cytosolic or nuclear receptors? (select three correct responses)

a.why: Testosterone, retinoic acid and vitamin D are lipid soluble and bind nuclear receptors. Antidiuretic hormone is a peptide (surface V1/V2 receptors); prostaglandin D acts on surface G-protein coupled receptors.
a.cite: LC21 transcript (steroids, vitamin D intracellular receptors)

stem: Natriuretic peptides (ANP & BNP) interact with an enzyme-linked cell surface receptor. What second messenger is generated by this enzyme? (select one correct response)

a.why: Natriuretic peptide receptors are membrane guanylyl cyclases that generate cyclic GMP, which activates protein kinase G. Trap: cyclic AMP comes from adenylyl cyclase.

stem: Which amino acid is critical to the activation / inactivation of insulin receptors and all of the growth factor receptors that were presented because of their autophosphorylation activities? (select one correct response)

a.why: Insulin and growth factor receptors are receptor tyrosine kinases; they autophosphorylate tyrosine residues, creating docking sites that activate the pathway.

stem: Of the receptor and second messenger pathways that have been presented in class, which receptor is associated with both the JAK/STAT pathway and the MAPK pathway? (select one correct response)

a.why: The erythropoietin receptor is a cytokine receptor that uses Janus kinase 2 / signal transducer and activator of transcription 5 and also recruits Grb2/SOS to activate RAS/MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase). Insulin lacks JAK/STAT.

stem: In an epithelial cell that expresses high amounts of active 11-β hydroxy steroid dehydrogenase 2 (11-β HSD 2), what naturally-occurring signaling molecule is used to enhance the expression of SGK1, ENaC, and ROMK? (select one correct response)

a.why: With cortisol inactivated to cortisone by 11-beta HSD2, aldosterone is the hormone that drives serum and glucocorticoid kinase 1, epithelial sodium channel and renal outer medullary potassium channel expression.

stem: In reference to question 20, what receptor is targeted selectively by the naturally-occurring agonist? (select one correct response)

a.why: Aldosterone selectively activates the mineralocorticoid receptor, which acts as a transcription factor. Angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors upstream in the adrenal, not here.

stem: If RAS is mutated so that it can bind, but not hydrolyze GTP, which two signaling pathways would appear to be overstimulated? (select two correct responses)
opts: Norepinephrine (β1) acting on cardiac pacemaker cells
Norepinephrine (α1) acting on vascular smooth muscle cells
Thyroid hormone (T3) acting on adipocytes in major fat pads
Fibroblast growth factor (FGF) acting on parenchymal fibroblast progenitor cells
Erythropoietin (EPO) acting on erythrocyte progenitor cells

a.why: GTPase-dead RAS stays on, overstimulating RAS/MAPK pathways: fibroblast growth factor (receptor tyrosine kinase) and erythropoietin (JAK/STAT plus RAS/MAPK). Beta-1 and alpha-1 use heterotrimeric G-proteins; tri-iodothyronine uses a nuclear receptor.

stem: Which of the newly discovered signaling molecules is more likely to have a receptor that is located on the surface of the target cells?
ctx: Use the following information to answer questions 23 through 26. Two new physiological signaling molecules, ‘new α’ and ‘new β’ are discovered. A biochemist begins to describe the biophysical characteristics of these novel signaling molecules. The octanol:water partition coefficients are 0.03 (logP=-1.5) and 75 (logP=1.9) for ‘new α’ and ‘new β’, respectively. (new α = 0.03; new β = 75; a larger number indicates that the solute dissolves more easily in lipid)

a.why: New alpha has log P -1.5: water-soluble, cannot cross the lipid bilayer, so its receptor must be on the cell surface.
a.cite: LC21 transcript (log P and receptor location)

stem: Both new α and new β are present in vascular circulation and appear to exhibit characteristics of endocrine signaling. Which of the newly discovered signaling molecules is more likely to be free in circulation (i.e., not associated with a carrier protein)?

a.why: Water-soluble new alpha dissolves in plasma and travels free; lipid-soluble new beta needs a carrier protein to stay in solution.

stem: Which of the newly discovered signaling molecules will have a larger reservoir of signaling molecules in circulation and is likely to have a longer half-life in circulation?

a.why: Carrier-bound new beta forms a circulating reservoir sequestered in the vasculature and protected from clearance and filtration, giving a longer half-life.

stem: Based on your answers to questions 23-25, which signaling molecule in the following list is most like ‘new β’?

a.why: Thyroxine is lipid soluble, travels on carrier proteins (thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin), has a long half-life and an intracellular receptor. The others are water-soluble with surface receptors.

stem: How many connexins must be in each of the adjoining cells to form one gap junction? (Select one correct answer.)

a.why: Each cell contributes one connexon, a hexamer of 6 connexins; the full gap junction channel has 12. 'In each of the adjoining cells' means 6.
a.flag: Wording 'in each cell' vs total (12) is the trap.

stem: Which of the following can move, by diffusion, through a gap junction? (Select all answers that are correct.)

a.why: Gap junctions pass molecules under about 1,000 daltons: cyclic nucleotides, glucose and nucleotides. Glycogen (a huge polymer) and ribosomes are far too large.

stem: In this scenario, which component is a cytosolic second messenger? (Select one correct answer.)
ctx: For questions 3-5: Leydig cells in the testes secrete testosterone into circulation. When exposed to testosterone, epithelial cells lining the vas deferens will express high levels of prostaglandin H synthase 2 (PTGS2 or COX2). Subsequently, when these cells are exposed to locally released bradykinin, they will secrete prostaglandin D (PGD) into the lumen and secrete prostaglandin E (PGE) into the interstitial fluid bathing the epithelial basolateral cell membranes. Here, PGE can interact with a G-protein coupled receptor (EP2) on these epithelial cells to stimulate adenylyl cyclase, generate cAMP, activate protein kinase A (PKA), phosphorylate an ion channel and ultimately secrete bicarbonate into the lumen.

a.why: Cyclic AMP is the small cytosolic second messenger made by adenylyl cyclase. EP2 is the receptor, protein kinase A is the effector enzyme, prostaglandin E is the first messenger.

stem: In this scenario, which component is signaling by an endocrine pathway? (Select one correct answer.)

a.why: Testosterone travels from Leydig cells through circulation to distant vas deferens epithelium: endocrine signaling.

stem: In this scenario, which component is signaling by an autocrine or paracrine pathway? (Select one correct answer.)

a.why: Prostaglandin E is released into interstitial fluid and acts on EP2 receptors on the same or neighboring epithelial cells: autocrine/paracrine. Testosterone is endocrine; cyclic AMP and protein kinase A are intracellular.

stem: In contact-dependent cell signaling, in what part of the cell is the signaling molecule typically located? (Select one correct answer.)

a.why: In contact-dependent signaling the signal (e.g., selectins, integrins, neurexin) is membrane-bound and binds a receptor on the touching cell's membrane.

stem: Which of the following is an example of paracrine signaling to a cytosolic enzyme ‘receptor’? (Select one correct answer.)
opts: Acetylcholine to a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAchR)
Testosterone to sex hormone binding protein

a.why: Nitric oxide diffuses from endothelium to nearby smooth muscle (paracrine) and binds soluble guanylyl cyclase, a cytosolic enzyme acting as receptor. Histamine/H1 and nicotinic receptors are membrane receptors.

stem: Which of the following has a large positive logP, associates with a carrier protein in circulation and has a cytosolic receptor? (Select one correct answer.)

a.why: 17-beta estradiol: log P about 4, carried on sex hormone-binding globulin, intracellular estrogen receptor. The others are water-soluble peptides or amines with surface receptors.

stem: Nuclear receptors and/or cytosolic receptors that migrate to the nucleus (e.g., mineralocorticoid receptor, MR) are associated with which type of cellular response? (Select one correct answer.)
opts: Adenylyl cyclase activation, cAMP generation and PKA activity
Gene transcription and protein synthesis (e.g., SGK, ENaC)
Guanylyl cyclase activation, cGMP generation and increased PKG activity
Phospholipase C activation, generation of IP₃ & DAG, Ca²⁺ release and PKC activation

a.why: Nuclear/cytosolic receptors such as the mineralocorticoid receptor are transcription factors: they drive gene transcription and protein synthesis (serum and glucocorticoid kinase, epithelial sodium channel). The other options are surface-receptor pathways.

stem: Which of the following are correct values for the typical concentration of free ionized Ca²⁺ in a cell at rest? (select two correct answers)

a.why: Resting free calcium = 100 nanomolar = 10^-4 millimolar; calcium is divalent, so equivalents are double (200 nanoequivalents/liter, 2x10^-4 milliequivalents/liter). 10^-6 molar is 1 micromolar, 10x too high.

stem: Which bonds hold complementary DNA bases together in the double helix?

a.why: Complementary bases pair by hydrogen bonds (adenine–thymine 2, guanine–cytosine 3). Covalent phosphodiester bonds hold the backbone of each strand, not the pairs.

stem: Which enzyme is able to connect the 3′ end of one DNA fragment to the 5′ end of another (e.g. in Okazaki fragments)?

a.why: DNA ligase seals the nick by forming a phosphodiester bond between a 3′ hydroxyl and a 5′ phosphate, joining Okazaki fragments. Polymerase only adds nucleotides; it cannot join two fragments.

stem: A cell lacking telomerase would most likely show:
opts: Increased Okazaki fragments and DNA fragmentation
Increased mutation rate and formation of tumors
Progressive chromosome shortening and cell senescence

a.why: Telomerase extends chromosome ends. Without it, the end-replication problem shortens telomeres each division until the cell senesces. Tumors are linked to telomerase being ON, not off.

stem: In diagnostic PCR, which component determines diagnostic specificity?

a.why: Primers bind only the target sequence, so they decide what gets amplified (specificity). Polymerase, nucleotides and dye are generic to any reaction.

stem: Which PCR component comes from the patient being diagnosed?

a.why: The template DNA is extracted from the patient sample; everything else (primers, polymerase, nucleotides, dye) is supplied in the kit.

stem: Which PCR component allows detection of replication?

a.why: In real-time (quantitative) polymerase chain reaction, an intercalating dye fluoresces when bound to double-stranded DNA, so signal rises as product copies accumulate.
a.flag: Marked select-all by extraction, but only one option fits.

stem: A patient sample produces a low Ct value on qPCR. What does this indicate?

a.why: Cycle threshold (Ct) = cycle when fluorescence crosses threshold. More starting target crosses sooner, so low Ct = high target DNA. Inverse relationship is the trap.

stem: Why is DNA more stable than RNA?
opts: DNA has deoxyribose and double-stranded structure
DNA contains uracil instead of thymine

a.why: Deoxyribose lacks the 2′ hydroxyl that lets RNA self-cleave, and the double helix protects bases. Option b is backwards: RNA has uracil, DNA has thymine.

stem: Which type of RNA is an important catalyst for translation?

a.why: Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is a ribozyme: it catalyzes peptide bond formation in the ribosome. Transfer RNA (tRNA) carries amino acids; messenger RNA (mRNA) is the template.

stem: Which type of RNA can reduce the translation of target genes?

a.why: MicroRNA (miRNA) base-pairs with target messenger RNA and blocks translation or triggers its degradation, reducing expression.

stem: Which modification allows differential expression of protein isoforms from one gene?

a.why: Alternative splicing joins different exon combinations from one pre-messenger RNA, producing multiple protein isoforms from one gene. Promoter methylation only changes how much is transcribed.
a.flag: RNA editing (c) can also yield isoforms (e.g., apolipoprotein B-100 vs B-48) and alternative polyadenylation can too; single best answer is a. Confirm against LC13 slides.

stem: Acetylation of histones generally results in:

a.why: Acetylation neutralizes positive lysines on histones, loosening their grip on negatively charged DNA → open euchromatin → more transcription.
a.flag: Marked select-all by extraction, but only one option fits.

stem: Which changes generally reduce transcription? (Select all that apply)

a.why: DNA methylation and histone deacetylation both compact chromatin (heterochromatin) and silence genes. Acetylation and euchromatin do the opposite.

stem: Which of the following enzymes have activity increased by phosphorylation? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Glycogen phosphorylase and hormone-sensitive lipase are switched ON by protein kinase A phosphorylation. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is turned OFF by phosphorylation; fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and phosphofructokinase-1 are allosteric, not phosphorylated.
a.cite: LC15 slides; LC18 slides; LC20 slides 12–14

stem: Which of the following enzymes have activity increased by dephosphorylation? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Glycogen synthase and the phosphofructokinase-2 (kinase) side of the bifunctional enzyme are active when dephosphorylated. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase side is active when phosphorylated; carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and glucokinase aren't phosphorylation-regulated.

stem: Which of the following enzymes would have activity increased by increased insulin signaling? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Insulin activates phosphatases: acetyl-CoA carboxylase, glycogen synthase and phosphofructokinase-2 turn on; fructose-2,6-bisphosphate rises → activates phosphofructokinase-1 and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (so b is out).
a.cite: LC18 slides; LC20 slides; LC23 transcript

stem: Which of the following enzymes would have activity increased by increased glucagon signaling? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Glucagon → protein kinase A phosphorylates: fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase side ON, glycogen phosphorylase ON, hormone-sensitive lipase ON. Glucokinase is an insulin-side enzyme.
a.cite: LC18 slides; LC20 slides 12–14; LC23 transcript
a.flag: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is regulated by N-acetylglutamate, not glucagon directly; fasting does raise urea cycle flux indirectly (outside: glucagon induces urea-cycle enzymes). Treated as a distractor.

stem: Which of the following enzymes would have activity increased by increased epinephrine signaling? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: In liver, epinephrine uses the same protein kinase A pathway as glucagon: bisphosphatase side ON → fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls → fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase disinhibited; glycogen phosphorylase and hormone-sensitive lipase ON.
a.flag: Including a (fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase) relies on the indirect fall in fructose-2,6-bisphosphate in liver; if the key wants only directly phosphorylated enzymes, answer is b,d,e.

stem: Which of the following enzymes would have activity increased by increased concentrations of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate?

a.why: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase-1, pushing glycolysis forward.

stem: Which of the following enzymes would have activity decreased by increased concentrations of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate?

a.why: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, so gluconeogenesis shuts down while glycolysis runs — reciprocal regulation.

stem: Which of the following enzymes would have activity increased by increased concentrations of citrate?

a.why: Citrate is a feed-forward activator of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (abundant citrate signals spare acetyl-CoA for fat synthesis). Trap: citrate INHIBITS phosphofructokinase-1.
a.cite: LC20 slides (feed-forward regulation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase)

stem: Which level of protein structure is determined directly by the sequence of amino acids?

a.why: Primary structure IS the amino acid sequence. Higher levels (folding) follow from it but are shaped by interactions, not directly 'the sequence'.

stem: The glucocorticoid receptor (GR) is inactive in the cytoplasm when bound to heat shock proteins (HSPs). What causes activation of the receptor?
opts: Binding of cortisol, which induces a conformational change in GR

a.why: Cortisol binds the glucocorticoid receptor, changing its conformation so it releases heat shock proteins 70/90 and moves to the nucleus. Ligand binding = conformational regulation.

stem: Which statement best explains the purpose of zymogen activation?
opts: It prevents premature enzyme activity that could damage cells
It allows reversible inhibition of enzymes
It promotes protein synthesis in response to stress

a.why: Zymogens (proenzymes, e.g., trypsinogen) are made inactive and cleaved only where needed, preventing proteases from digesting the cell that made them.

stem: Which post-translational modifications can regulate protein activity? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Phosphorylation, methylation, glycosylation and proteolytic cleavage all modify proteins after translation. RNA splicing acts on messenger RNA before translation, so it isn't post-translational.
a.cite: LC15 slides (phosphorylation, cleavage); outside course materials (methylation, glycosylation)

stem: Which glucose transporter is insulin-dependent and primarily responsible for glucose uptake into skeletal muscle?

a.why: Glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4) moves to the membrane in response to insulin in skeletal muscle and adipose. GLUT2 is the insulin-independent liver/pancreas transporter.

stem: During anaerobic metabolism, the reduction of pyruvate to lactate allows:
opts: Regeneration of NAD+ for continued glycolysis

a.why: Lactate dehydrogenase uses NADH to reduce pyruvate, regenerating nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) needed by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase so glycolysis continues. No extra ATP is made.
a.flag: Marked select-all by extraction, but only one option fits.

stem: Which are benefits of anaerobic metabolism via lactate production? (select ALL that apply)
opts: Allows rapid ATP production without oxygen
Supports brief bursts of muscle activity
Increases total ATP yield per glucose molecule

a.why: Lactate production regenerates NAD+, allows fast ATP without oxygen for muscle bursts, and lactate feeds hepatic gluconeogenesis (Cori cycle). It LOWERS ATP yield per glucose (2 ATP only).

stem: Why is the TCA cycle considered an aerobic pathway?
opts: Oxygen is required to regenerate NAD+ and FAD in the electron transport system
Oxygen is consumed in the conversion of citrate to isocitrate
Oxygen directly oxidizes pyruvate in the mitochondrial matrix

a.why: No tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle step uses oxygen, but it needs NAD+ and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), which are regenerated only when the electron transport system passes electrons to oxygen.

stem: Which of the following best explains the metabolic consequence of oxygen deprivation (ischemia) on the TCA cycle?
opts: The TCA cycle continues normally, producing lactate
NAD+ accumulates, inhibiting the TCA cycle
NADH accumulates, reversing part of the TCA cycle
FADH2 levels drop, increasing ATP yield

a.why: Without oxygen, NADH builds up (NAD+ depleted); step 8 (malate dehydrogenase) runs in reverse to regenerate NAD+, and steps 6–8 run backward, accumulating succinate.

stem: Why is ischemia dangerous to cells?
opts: Oxygen accumulation in mitochondria causes oxidative damage to proteins and lipids.
The cell runs out of ATP, which leads to loss of membrane integrity.
The concentration of succinate builds up to a toxic level, damaging the mitochondria.
The lack of oxygen prevents glycolysis from occurring, stopping all ATP production.

a.why: No oxygen → no oxidative ATP → sodium-potassium ATPase fails → cells swell and lose membrane integrity. Succinate build-up causes damage on REPERFUSION (oxidative surge), not as a toxin during ischemia.

stem: Which conditions would cause the TCA cycle to slow down or reverse direction? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Low oxygen and a high NADH-to-NAD+ ratio stall the dehydrogenases and drive the reversible end steps backward. More oxaloacetate or more ADP speeds the cycle.

stem: In the liver, the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase is required for:
opts: Adding phosphate to glucose for trapping
Dephosphorylating glucose for export into the blood

a.why: Glucose-6-phosphatase removes the phosphate so free glucose can leave liver cells via glucose transporter 2. Muscle lacks it, so muscle glycogen can't raise blood glucose.

stem: Which amino acids are exclusively ketogenic?

a.why: Leucine and lysine yield only acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate, never gluconeogenic carbon. Phenylalanine, tyrosine and isoleucine are both glucogenic and ketogenic.

stem: Which of the following is true of branched-chain amino acids (BCAA)?
opts: They are primarily catabolized by the liver
They can be directly converted into glucose
They are metabolized mainly by skeletal muscle

a.why: Branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) are preferentially catabolized by skeletal muscle; aromatic amino acids by liver.

stem: Which molecule is the direct allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the urea cycle?

a.why: N-acetylglutamate is the obligate allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. Glutamate is its precursor (via N-acetylglutamate synthetase), not the direct activator.
a.flag: Marked select-all by extraction, but only one option fits.

stem: Which effects occur during increased amino acid catabolism, such as fasting or high-protein diets? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: More amino acid breakdown → more transamination → glutamate RISES → more N-acetylglutamate → urea cycle up → more urea excreted. Decreased glutamate (d) is backwards.

stem: Which statement best explains why fatty acid oxidation cannot fully support gluconeogenesis?
opts: Acetyl-CoA carbons are lost as CO₂ and cannot form oxaloacetate
Fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria during fasting
β-oxidation consumes NAD+ instead of producing it

a.why: Acetyl-CoA's two carbons enter the tricarboxylic acid cycle and two carbons leave as carbon dioxide, so there's no net oxaloacetate to make glucose (pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible).
a.cite: LC20 slides; outside course materials (standard biochemistry)

stem: Which diagnostic test probes a tissue section with labeled antibodies?

a.why: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) applies labeled antibodies to a tissue section (classic: rabies). Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) runs on serum in wells.

stem: Why can the ELISA for EIA produce more false positives than the Coggins test?
opts: The ELISA lacks a wash step

a.why: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) amplifies signal enzymatically, making it more sensitive than Coggins (agglutination/precipitation) for equine infectious anemia (EIA) — but more false positives, so confirm with Coggins.

stem: Why are antibodies ideal diagnostic tools?
opts: They bind DNA sequences with high selectivity
They bind unique 3D protein conformations with high selectivity
They require denatured proteins to achieve specificity

a.why: Antibodies recognize a specific three-dimensional shape (epitope) on a folded protein, giving high selectivity. They don't bind DNA sequences and generally need native, not denatured, conformation.

stem: Enzymes accelerate reactions by:

a.why: Enzymes lower activation energy by stabilizing the transition state. They don't change free energy change (ΔG) or the equilibrium.

stem: Which of the following quantities helps predict how fast a reaction will proceed?

a.why: Activation energy (Ea) predicts rate: higher Ea = slower. Free energy change (ΔG) predicts direction only, not speed.

stem: Which of the following enzymes has a high Km relative to its isozyme, allowing efficient storage of glucose at higher concentrations?

a.why: Glucokinase (liver) has a high Michaelis constant (Km ~15 mM), so it works mainly when glucose is high — storing excess after meals. Hexokinase has low Km/high affinity.
a.flag: Marked select-all by extraction, but only one option fits.

stem: In equine polysaccharide storage myopathy (EPSM Type 1), glycogen synthase remains active even when glucose-6-phosphate is low. Which regulatory process has failed?

a.why: Glucose-6-phosphate is an earlier pathway intermediate that activates the later enzyme glycogen synthase = feed-forward activation; the equine mutation (R309H) leaves the enzyme active without it.
a.flag: Feed-forward activation is a type of allosteric activation, so c is technically also true; slide frames it as feed-forward, so b is the best answer.

stem: What mechanism is activated during early fasting to maintain glucose homeostasis when exogenous glucose uptake starts to drop?

a.why: Early fasting (meal absorbed) → moderate glucagon → liver glycogenolysis is the main blood glucose source. Gluconeogenesis takes over in late fasting.

stem: What process is strongly upregulated during starvation?

a.why: Starvation = gluconeogenic substrates run out; gluconeogenesis falls and ketone bodies rise dramatically. Ketosis is the hallmark of starvation.

stem: What metabolic change marks the transition from early to late fasting?

a.why: Postprandial→early fasting = dietary glucose gone; early→late fasting = glycogen gone; late fasting→starvation = gluconeogenic substrates gone.

stem: Which hormone tends to increase energy availability in response to stressful stimuli?

a.why: Epinephrine (sympathetic 'fight or flight') mobilizes glucose and fat regardless of fed state; in liver it uses the glucagon pathway. Glucagon responds to low glucose, not stress.

stem: Why can’t fat be burned efficiently for energy without sufficient glucose?
opts: Low glucose causes low NAD+ which prevents the TCA cycle from running
Low glucose causes oxaloacetate to be used for gluconeogenesis instead of the TCA cycle
Low glucose causes succinate to build up in the TCA cycle disrupting the electron transport system
Low glucose decreases acetyl-CoA from β-oxidation, limiting substrate for the TCA cycle

a.why: Oxaloacetate is shared: when glucose is low, gluconeogenesis drains it, so acetyl-CoA from fat can't enter the tricarboxylic acid cycle. 'Burning fat efficiently requires glucose.'

stem: What is the purpose of ketogenesis?
opts: To allow efficient utilization of lipid energy
To regulate the pH of the blood during ischemia
To replenish free coenzyme A in the absence of the TCA cycle
To replenish NAD+ in the absence of the electron transport system

a.why: Ketogenesis regenerates free coenzyme A when acetyl-CoA can't enter the tricarboxylic acid cycle (oxaloacetate depleted). Fuel for brain/heart is a bonus, not the primary purpose.
a.flag: Option a is tempting; Dr. Basil's slides and lecture explicitly frame ketogenesis as replenishing coenzyme A.

stem: What normally prevents significant ketogenesis during late fasting?
opts: Activation of citrate synthase by glucagon reduces the concentration of acetyl-CoA
Continued insulin signaling maintains acetyl-CoA carboxylase activity
Decreased β-oxidation reduces acetyl-CoA availability for ketone synthesis

a.why: In late fasting, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids keep gluconeogenesis and oxaloacetate supplied, so acetyl-CoA still enters the cycle; ketones stay minimal. Insulin is very low then, so c is wrong.
a.flag: Marked select-all by extraction, but only one option fits.

stem: Which of the following is a volatile fatty acid that is an important gluconeogenic substrate for ruminants?

a.why: Propionate is the only gluconeogenic volatile fatty acid (enters via succinyl-CoA). Acetate and butyrate are ketogenic/lipogenic; alanine and lysine aren't volatile fatty acids.

stem: Which DNA base pair has the highest binding energy?

a.why: Guanine–cytosine pairs share three hydrogen bonds (adenine–thymine two), so they have the highest binding energy. A–C and G–T aren't normal Watson–Crick pairs.

stem: How does the recognition step happen in DNA replication?
opts: A DNA polymerase coenzyme recruits the correct dNTP
DNA polymerase actively recruits the correct dNTP
dNTPs enter by simple diffusion and selection happens by hydrogen bonding

a.why: Deoxynucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) diffuse into the active site; the correct one is selected by complementary hydrogen bonding with the template base. The polymerase doesn't actively recruit them, and no coenzyme does.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: Which enzyme initiates replication by synthesizing short strands of RNA?

a.why: DNA primase lays down the short ribonucleic acid (RNA) primer that DNA polymerase extends; DNA polymerase cannot start a strand from nothing. RNA polymerase is for transcription, not replication.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: Which component of a PCR reaction gives selectivity for replicating a specific DNA sequence?

a.why: Primers are complementary to the target sequence, so they decide which stretch gets amplified in polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Taq polymerase and nucleotides copy anything; the DNA is the patient template.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: You are running a PCR diagnostic test for EHV1. Which of the following samples would be a weak positive sample for EHV1?

a.why: Cycle threshold (Ct) is inversely related to target amount. Ct 28 = detected but late = weak positive. Ct 5 = strong positive; Ct well over 35 = negative.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: Which of the following components of a gene are found in the mature mRNA?

a.why: Mature messenger RNA (mRNA) keeps the exons; introns are spliced out. Promoters, enhancers and repressor sequences are DNA regulatory regions that are never part of the transcript.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: How is the second X chromosome in female mammals often silenced?
opts: It is not replicated in normal cells

a.why: The inactive X (Barr body) is heavily methylated (and its histones deacetylated), packing it as silent heterochromatin. Acetylation does the opposite, opening chromatin. It is still replicated.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)
a.flag: Option 'methylate' typo for 'methylated'.

stem: Which type of RNA is an important catalyst for translation?

a.why: Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is the catalyst (a ribozyme) that forms peptide bonds in the ribosome. Transfer RNA (tRNA) carries amino acids; messenger RNA (mRNA) is the template.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: Which type of RNA can reduce the translation of target genes?

a.why: MicroRNA (miRNA) binds complementary target messenger RNA and blocks its translation or triggers its degradation, reducing gene expression.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: Which amino acid is most likely to carry a negative charge at normal serum pH?

a.why: Glutamate has a side-chain carboxyl group (pKa about 4) that is deprotonated and negative at blood pH 7.4. Histidine is the tempting one, but it is neutral or positive; isoleucine and threonine are uncharged.
a.cite: LC14 slide 6 (amino acid side chains); outside course materials for pKa

stem: Which level of protein structure is important for creating locally stable structures in a protein usually stabilized by hydrogen bonding along the amide backbone?

a.why: Secondary structure (alpha helix, beta sheet) = locally stable folds held by hydrogen bonds along the amide backbone. Tertiary is global collapse driven by hydrophobic side-chain interactions.
a.flag: Marked multiple-select but only one answer fits.

stem: Which diagnostic test uses an antibody to probe a tissue slide for the presence of antigens?

a.why: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses a labeled antibody to find a specific antigen (protein) in a tissue section on a slide.

stem: Which diagnostic test uses an antigen to detect the presence of antibodies in serum and uses an enzyme to multiply the signal?

a.why: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) links an enzyme to an antigen or antibody so each binding event produces lots of signal. Agglutination has no enzyme.

stem: Which diagnostic test uses an antigen to precipitate antibodies in serum?

a.why: Agglutination: antigen added to serum cross-links specific antibodies so they clump and precipitate. No enzyme amplification (that's enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay).

stem: What causes the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) to dissociate from the neutralizing HSP complex?
opts: A conformational change in GR caused by cortisol binding
Cleavage of HSP70 by a cortisol-activated protease
Degradation of HSP90 by the proteosome

a.why: Cortisol diffuses in and binds the glucocorticoid receptor (GR), changing its shape so it releases from the heat shock protein (HSP90/HSP70) complex, dimerizes, and enters the nucleus. No cleavage or degradation is involved.

stem: What is the name for a protein that is synthesized in an inactive form and must be cleaved to be active?

a.why: A zymogen is an inactive precursor that must be proteolytically cleaved to become active (e.g., trypsinogen to trypsin). Promoter and enhancer are DNA sequences.

stem: Which of the following quantities describes how sensitive an enzyme is to substrate concentrations?

a.why: Michaelis constant (Km) = substrate concentration at half maximal velocity; near Km, rate changes a lot with substrate, so it measures substrate sensitivity/affinity. Maximal velocity (Vmax) is the ceiling, not sensitivity.

stem: Which of the following quantities predicts how quickly a reaction will proceed?

a.why: Activation energy (Ea) predicts how fast a reaction proceeds (higher Ea = slower). Gibbs free energy change (ΔG) only predicts direction, not speed — the classic trap.

stem: An allosteric site in an enzyme is described as the site where:
opts: Enzyme activity can be controlled away from the active site
The enzyme is linked to the cytoskeleton
The reactants bind and are converted to products

a.why: Allosteric site = a regulatory site away from the active site where activators or inhibitors bind and change activity. Option d describes the active site; c describes zymogen activation.
a.flag: Marked multiple-select but only one option is correct.

stem: Which of the following glucose transporters helps move glucose up its concentration gradient in the small intestine to allow efficient absorption of glucose from the diet?

a.why: Sodium-glucose linked transporter 1 (SGLT1) is secondary active: it uses the sodium gradient to move glucose up its concentration gradient in the intestine. GLUT (glucose transporter) 1, 3, 4 are passive.
a.flag: Marked multiple-select but only one answer fits.

stem: Which of the following enzymes is expressed in the liver and allows the liver to store glucose at high concentrations and export glucose at low concentrations?

a.why: Glucokinase (liver) has high Km and no product inhibition, so it traps glucose only when blood glucose is high and lets the liver release glucose when low. Hexokinase has low Km and works everywhere.
a.flag: Marked multiple-select; only glucokinase fits. GLUT4 and SGLT1 aren't enzymes.

stem: Which enzyme is sensitive to feed-forward activation from fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to allow coordinated regulation of glycolysis?

a.why: Pyruvate kinase is feed-forward activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, the product of phosphofructokinase-1, so the end of glycolysis keeps pace with the committed step. Phosphofructokinase-1 makes it, not responds to it.
a.flag: Marked multiple-select; single answer.

stem: Which enzyme is allosterically activated by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate to increase glycolysis during high insulin signaling?

a.why: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate allosterically activates phosphofructokinase-1 (and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase). Insulin dephosphorylates phosphofructokinase-2 so more fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is made.
a.flag: Marked multiple-select; single answer.

stem: During intense anaerobic exercise, what is the main energy source for the heart?

a.why: The heart stays oxygenated, so it takes up the lactic acid pouring out of anaerobic muscle and oxidizes it; Dr. Basil: during a run ~80% of heart energy is lactic acid.

stem: Why are the first three steps in the TCA cycle O2 dependent?
opts: Production of two molecules of CO2 requires O2
The final step in the cycle produces NADH and has a +ΔG
The first step in the cycle produces NADH
The third step in the cycle requires O2 as a reactant

a.why: Step 1 needs oxaloacetate from step 8 (malate to oxaloacetate), which has a large positive ΔG and produces NADH. Without oxygen, NADH builds up, step 8 runs backward, oxaloacetate depletes. No O2 used directly.

stem: What intermediate in the TCA cycle builds up during ischemia?

a.why: In ischemia, steps 6–8 run backward (to regenerate NAD+), so fumarate is converted to succinate and succinate accumulates.

stem: In the reaction: 2NADH + O2 + 2 H+ → 2 NAD+ + 2 H2O Which molecule is being reduced?

a.why: Oxygen gains electrons (becomes water), so O2 is reduced. NADH is oxidized to NAD+ (it's the reducing agent) — don't flip which is oxidized vs reduced.

stem: Which complex in the electron transport system catalyzes the oxidation of NADH?

a.why: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) oxidizes NADH and passes electrons to coenzyme Q. Complex II is succinate dehydrogenase (FADH2 route).

stem: During reperfusion, why does the succinate stored during ischemia cause oxidative damage?
opts: Loss of the proton gradient during ischemia reduces the ability to synthesize ATP
Excess production of FADH2 and reduced coenzyme Q causes complex I to run backwards
Introduction of O2 allows complex IV to produce water rapidly

a.why: On reperfusion, stored succinate is rapidly oxidized at complex II, over-reducing coenzyme Q; electrons are pushed backward through complex I, which leaks a superoxide burst (reverse electron transport). Option c is normal and harmless.

stem: Why is it necessary to store energy as glycogen instead of just as fat? (select all that apply)
opts: Fatty acids cannot be mobilized for energy as quickly
Fatty acids increase the osmolarity of the solution
Fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose
Fatty acids cannot be used anaerobically

a.why: Glycogen mobilizes faster than fat, fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose, and glycogen-derived glucose can be used anaerobically. b is false: free glucose (not fat) is the osmolyte problem.

stem: Which hormones would tend to increase the activity of glycogen phosphorylase (select all that apply)

a.why: Epinephrine and glucagon activate protein kinase A, which (via phosphorylase kinase) phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase. Insulin activates phosphatases, inactivating it. Aldosterone and parathyroid hormone aren't glycogen regulators.

stem: Which hormones would tend to increase the activity of glycogen synthase (select all that apply)

a.why: Insulin activates protein phosphatases, dephosphorylating and activating glycogen synthase. Epinephrine and glucagon phosphorylate (inactivate) it.

stem: Which of the following compounds is a very important gluconeogenic substrate for runimants?

a.why: Propionate (from rumen fermentation) enters as succinyl-coenzyme A and is the main gluconeogenic substrate in ruminants. Acetate and palmitate yield only acetyl-coenzyme A, which can't make net glucose.
a.flag: 'runimants' typo for ruminants.

stem: Which hormones would tend to reduce the concentration of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate in the liver? (select all that apply)

a.why: Glucagon and epinephrine activate protein kinase A, which phosphorylates phosphofructokinase-2/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase, turning on the phosphatase side, so fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls. Insulin raises it.

stem: Which amino acids cannot be used for gluconeogenesis? (select all that apply)

a.why: Leucine and lysine are strictly ketogenic (only acetyl-coenzyme A/acetoacetate). Isoleucine, phenylalanine and tyrosine are both ketogenic and glucogenic.

stem: Which amino acids would be preferentially metabolized by the liver during first past metabolism? (select all that apply)

a.why: Aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine, tyrosine) are preferentially metabolized by the liver on first pass. Branched-chain (isoleucine, leucine; also valine) are catabolized mainly in muscle. Lysine is neither group.

stem: Liver failure can cause which of the following amino acid metabolism disturbances? (select all that apply)
opts: Increased circulating aromatic amino acid concentration

a.why: Failing liver can't clear aromatic amino acids (they rise), so the branched-chain:aromatic ratio falls (~3:1 to ~1.5:1), and the urea cycle fails so ammonium rises.

stem: Excessive metabolism of ketogenic amino acids would reduce the concentration of what important intermediate in the liver?

a.why: Ketogenic amino acid breakdown traps coenzyme A as acetyl-coenzyme A, depleting free coenzyme A (HS-CoA); ketogenesis regenerates it. Acetyl-coenzyme A rises, not falls.

stem: Which of the following is a form of nitrogen waste produced by the liver that muscle cells use to store high energy phosphate bonds?

a.why: Creatine is an alternate nitrogen waste the liver makes; muscle phosphorylates it to creatine phosphate to store high-energy phosphate. Creatinine is its breakdown product excreted by kidneys.

stem: Why can’t fat be burned efficiently for energy without sufficient glucose?
opts: Low glucose causes low NAD+ which prevents the TCA cycle from running
Low glucose causes oxaloacetate to be used for gluconeogenesis instead of the TCA cycle
Low glucose causes succinate to build up in the TCA cycle disrupting the electron transport system

a.why: Fat yields acetyl-coenzyme A, which needs oxaloacetate to enter the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. Low glucose pulls oxaloacetate into gluconeogenesis, so acetyl-coenzyme A backs up into ketones.

stem: Which of the following would tend to increase the activity of acetyl-coA carboxylase? (select all that apply)

a.why: Citrate is the feed-forward activator, and insulin activates phosphatases that dephosphorylate (activate) acetyl-coenzyme A carboxylase. Adenosine monophosphate (via AMP-activated kinase), epinephrine and glucagon (via protein kinase A) phosphorylate and inhibit it.

stem: Which of the following would tend to increase the activity of hormone sensitive lipase? (select all that apply)

a.why: Hormone-sensitive lipase is activated by phosphorylation: adenosine monophosphate (AMP-activated kinase), epinephrine and glucagon (protein kinase A). Insulin dephosphorylates/inhibits it; citrate signals storage.
a.flag: Course slide/transcript say AMP-activated kinase phosphorylation activates HSL. Standard biochemistry says AMP-activated kinase actually inhibits HSL — answer with the course (a,c,d) on this exam.

stem: T or F: Ketone bodies are a pure waste product that can’t be used for anything in the body.

a.why: False. Ketone bodies are fuel for heart, muscle, brain and kidney (via 3-oxoacid coenzyme A transferase); only in excess do they cause ketoacidosis. Liver makes but can't use them.

stem: T or F: No portion of triglycerides can be used for gluconeogenesis.

a.why: False. The glycerol backbone of triglycerides is a gluconeogenic substrate (via dihydroxyacetone phosphate). Only the even-chain fatty acids can't make net glucose.

stem: What mechanism is activated during early fasting to maintain glucose homeostasis when exogenous glucose uptake starts to drop?

a.why: Early fasting (meal absorbed, no gut glucose): falling insulin and moderate glucagon trigger liver glycogenolysis as the main blood glucose source.

stem: What process is strongly upregulated during starvation?

a.why: In starvation gluconeogenic substrates run out, gluconeogenesis falls off and ketone bodies rise dramatically — ketosis is the hallmark of starvation.
a.flag: Lipolysis also continues, but Dr. Basil names ketogenesis/ketosis as the starvation hallmark.

stem: What metabolic change marks the transition from early to late fasting?

a.why: Early to late fasting = running out of glycogen. Postprandial to early = gut glucose gone; late fasting to starvation = gluconeogenic substrates gone.

stem: Which hormone tends to increase energy availability in response to stressful stimuli?

a.why: Epinephrine (sympathetic, fight-or-flight) mobilizes glucose and fatty acids in response to stress. Glucagon responds to low blood glucose, not stress.

stem: Which nucleotide pair has the most binding energy?

a.why: Guanine–cytosine pairs form three hydrogen bonds (adenine–thymine only two), so G-C has the most binding energy. A-C and G-A aren't Watson–Crick pairs.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: Which enzyme synthesizes a short complementary RNA strand to start replication?

a.why: DNA primase synthesizes the short ribonucleic acid (RNA) primer that starts replication; DNA polymerase then extends it.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: Which component of a PCR reaction gives selectivity for replicating a specific DNA sequence?

a.why: Primers bind only their complementary target sequence, giving polymerase chain reaction (PCR) its specificity. Taq polymerase and nucleotides are nonspecific; the DNA is the sample template.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: When using PCR as a diagnostic test, samples that have a higher Ct value are generally:
opts: More positive for the assayed target
Less positive for the assayed target

a.why: Higher cycle threshold (Ct) = more cycles needed to detect = less starting target = less positive.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: What is the purpose of the 3’ poly-A tail?
opts: Target the mRNA to the ribosome

a.why: The 3' poly-adenine (poly-A) tail protects messenger RNA from exonuclease degradation, extending its lifespan (and aids export/translation). It doesn't recruit RNA polymerase.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: A chromosome that has been highly methylated will likely:
opts: Have low transcription rates and express few genes
Have high transcription rates and express many genes
Have lower rates of DNA replication

a.why: Heavy DNA methylation compacts chromatin into heterochromatin, silencing genes: low transcription. Replication still occurs.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: Which type of RNA translates the codon code in RNA to an amino acid?

a.why: Transfer RNA (tRNA) reads the codon with its anticodon and carries the matching amino acid — the adapter. Ribosomal RNA catalyzes peptide bonds; messenger RNA carries the code.
a.cite: outside course materials (earlier exam, Lecture 10–13 nucleic acids)

stem: Which type of translational regulation can allow two closely related proteins to be produced from the same gene?

a.why: Differential (alternative) splicing joins different exons from one pre-messenger RNA, giving closely related protein isoforms from one gene. eIF2 (eukaryotic initiation factor 2) inhibition and micro-RNA reduce amount, not variety.
a.flag: Splicing is technically post-transcriptional, not translational, regulation — wording loose in original.

stem: Which of the following amino acids would be expected to be hydrophilic but have little charge at physiological pH (~pH 7)?

a.why: Serine has a polar hydroxyl (–OH) side chain: hydrophilic but uncharged at pH 7. Arginine (+) and glutamate (−) are charged; methionine is nonpolar/hydrophobic.

stem: Stable associations of multiple peptides to form a functional protein is known as:

a.why: Quaternary structure = stable association of two or more separate polypeptide chains into one functional protein (e.g., hemoglobin). Tertiary is the 3D fold of a single chain.

stem: Testing whether diluted serum from a patient can precipitate e. coli would be an example of what type of diagnostic test?

a.why: Agglutination assay: an antigen (here E. coli) is mixed with diluted (titered) serum; antibodies in the serum clump and precipitate it. Higher titer = more antibody.

stem: Using antibodies to identify and visualize PRRS virus on a slide of a biopsy from the small intestine would be an example of what type of diagnostic test?

a.why: Immunohistochemistry (IHC): an antibody probes a tissue section for a specific protein (here PRRS = porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus). ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) uses wells/serum, not tissue slides.
a.flag: Marked multi-select, but only one option fits.

stem: What causes the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) to dissociate from the neutralizing HSP complex?
opts: A conformational change in GR caused by cortisol binding
Cleavage of HSP70 by a cortisol-activated protease
Degradation of HSP90 by the proteosome

a.why: Cortisol binds the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) and changes its conformation, so it can no longer bind heat shock proteins 70 and 90 (HSP70/HSP90) and diffuses away. No protease or proteasome step.

stem: What causes the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) to enter the nucleus?
opts: Cleavage of GR by a cortisol-activated protease allows nuclear entry
Cortisol causes a change in nuclear membrane potential allowing nuclear entry
Cortisol causes nuclear pores to open
GR dimerization exposes a nuclear target peptide

a.why: After release from the heat shock protein complex, GR dimerizes; the shape change plus dimerization exposes/completes a nuclear localization (target) sequence that carries it into the nucleus.

stem: What causes glucocorticoid receptor (GR) signaling to quickly reduce when cortisol levels are reduced?
opts: Conformational change of GR when cortisol dissociates
Degradation of GR by the proteasome
Export of GR from the nucleus

a.why: GR in the nucleus is constantly ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome. When cortisol falls, no new GR enters, so nuclear GR is rapidly cleared and signaling stops.

stem: Which of the following quantities helps predict how quickly a reaction will proceed?

a.why: Activation energy (Ea) predicts how fast a reaction proceeds (higher Ea = slower). ΔG (Gibbs free energy change) predicts direction, not speed. KM = Michaelis constant (affinity).

stem: Which of the following quantities helps predict which direction a reaction will proceed?

a.why: ΔG (Gibbs free energy change) predicts direction: negative ΔG runs forward, positive runs in reverse. Activation energy (Ea) predicts speed; KD and KM describe binding affinity.

stem: What is an allosteric site on an enzyme?
opts: A regulatory location away from the active site
The active location where the reaction is catalyzed
The location where the substrate binds

a.why: Allosteric site = regulatory site away from the active site where activators/inhibitors bind and change enzyme activity. Substrate binding and catalysis happen at the active site.
a.flag: Marked multi-select, but only one option is correct.

stem: A loss-of-function mutation in phosphofructokinase 1 would likely result in the most severe damage in which tissue?

a.why: Red blood cells lack mitochondria, so anaerobic glycolysis is their only ATP source; losing phosphofructokinase 1 (PFK1) cripples them (hemolysis). Liver/kidney can burn fat and amino acids.
a.cite: LC16 transcript (red blood cells 100% glucose dependent); PFK deficiency in Springer spaniels = outside course materials

stem: Which transporter is able to actively move glucose up its concentration gradient?

a.why: Sodium-glucose linked transporter 1 (SGLT1) is secondary active: uses the sodium gradient to move glucose uphill (intestine, kidney). GLUT (glucose transporter) 1, 2, 4 are passive facilitated diffusion.

stem: What is the primary regulatory enzyme for glycolysis?

a.why: Phosphofructokinase 1 (PFK1) is the main regulatory (committed, irreversible) step of glycolysis. Hexokinase/glucokinase trap glucose but glucose-6-phosphate has other fates.

stem: What compound activates (is an allosteric activator of) the primary regulatory enzyme for glycolysis (from the previous question)?

a.why: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, made by phosphofructokinase 2 under insulin, is the potent allosteric activator of PFK1. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is PFK1's product, not its activator.
a.flag: Marked multi-select, but only one option is correct.

stem: Anaerobic metabolism by microorganisms in the healthy rumen should produce:

a.why: Healthy rumen microbes ferment to volatile fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate). Lactate accumulation = grain overload/rumen acidosis, not healthy.

stem: What organ can take up lactate and convert it back into glucose during intense exercise?

a.why: Liver takes up muscle lactate, converts it via lactate dehydrogenase to pyruvate, then glucose by gluconeogenesis (Cori cycle), returning glucose to muscle.

stem: Depletion of which intermediate during ischemia causes the reversible reactions of the TCA cycle to reverse and produce succinate?

a.why: Without oxygen, NAD+ is depleted, so reversible step 8 (malate dehydrogenase) runs backward to regenerate NAD+, and steps 6–8 reverse to succinate. Oxaloacetate depletion is the consequence, not the trigger.
a.flag: Oxaloacetate also depletes during ischemia (slide 25), but slide says NAD+ depletion drives the reversal.

stem: T/F – During reperfusion, lack of NAD+ causes disruption of the electron transport system and oxidative damage.

a.why: False. Reperfusion damage comes from stored succinate flooding complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) with electrons, pushing them backward into complex I and causing a superoxide burst — not lack of NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide).

stem: Which of the compounds is acting as an oxidizer and is being reduced in the following reaction? Cl2 + H2 → 2 H+ + 2 Cl-

a.why: Chlorine gas (Cl2) gains electrons (becomes Cl−): it is the oxidizer and is reduced. Hydrogen (H2) loses electrons: the reducer, oxidized. Cl− and H+ are products.

stem: Which complex in the electron transport system reduces oxygen to water?

a.why: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) passes electrons from cytochrome c to oxygen, reducing ½O2 to water.

stem: Why do we store glycogen instead of glucose in the liver?
opts: Glucose is too acidic to be stored
Glucose doesn’t have enough energy density

a.why: Glucose is an osmolyte: storing lots of it would pull water in and swell cells. Glycogen is insoluble, so it adds no osmotic pressure.

stem: What is the main regulatory enzyme for glycogen synthesis?

a.why: Glycogen synthase is the regulated step of glycogen synthesis (active when dephosphorylated; activated by glucose-6-phosphate). Branching enzyme and glucokinase are not the control point.

stem: Signaling from which of these hormones would increase the activity of glycogen synthase?

a.why: Insulin activates protein phosphatases that dephosphorylate (activate) glycogen synthase. Glucagon and epinephrine activate protein kinase A, which phosphorylates (inactivates) it.

stem: Which of the following compounds is an important gluconeogenic substrate in ruminants?

a.why: Propionate, a volatile fatty acid from rumen fermentation, enters as succinyl-CoA → oxaloacetate and is the ruminant's major gluconeogenic substrate. Glycerol is gluconeogenic but minor; palmitate is not.
