stem: Which of these enzymes is the main regulatory enzyme for gluconeogenesis?

a.why: None listed is correct. The main regulatory enzyme of gluconeogenesis is fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (inhibited by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate). Phosphofructokinase 1 and pyruvate kinase are glycolytic; glycogen phosphorylase is glycogenolysis.
a.flag: Answer choices omit fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase; 'glucose-6-phosphorylase' is not a real enzyme (likely meant glucose-6-phosphatase, which is not the main regulator). Ask Dr. Basil what was keyed.

stem: Signaling from which of these hormones would increase the activity of the main regulatory enzyme for gluconeogenesis?

a.why: Glucagon → protein kinase A phosphorylates PFK2/FBPase2 (phosphofructokinase 2/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase), turning on the phosphatase side; fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls, releasing inhibition of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.

stem: Which of the following amino acids is solely ketogenic?

a.why: Lysine (and leucine) are the only strictly ketogenic amino acids — they yield only acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate. Isoleucine is both glucogenic and ketogenic; glycine and serine are glucogenic.

stem: Why do elevated ammonium levels cause neurological issues?
opts: Ammonium is an antagonist of the glutamate receptor
Ammonium is an antagonist of the NMDA receptor

a.why: Ammonium (NH4+) is nearly the same size and charge as potassium, so it disrupts potassium channels that set neuronal resting potential. It also alkalinizes and boosts astrocyte glutamine synthesis.

stem: Which of the following nitrogen waste products is used by muscle to store high-energy phosphate bonds?

a.why: Creatine is an alternate nitrogen waste muscle uses to store high-energy phosphate (phosphocreatine). Creatinine is its breakdown product, excreted, not a store.

stem: What is the primary regulatory enzyme for lipogenesis?

a.why: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA: the committed, rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis (lipogenesis). Hormone-sensitive lipase controls lipolysis.

stem: Signaling from which of these hormones would increase the activity of the regulatory enzyme for lipogenesis?

a.why: Insulin activates phosphatases that dephosphorylate (activate) acetyl-CoA carboxylase. Glucagon (protein kinase A) and AMP-activated protein kinase phosphorylate and inhibit it.

stem: What is the primary regulatory enzyme for lipolysis?

a.why: Hormone-sensitive lipase releases fatty acids from stored triglyceride: the regulated step of lipolysis. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is lipogenesis.

stem: Signaling from which of these hormones would increase the activity of the regulatory enzyme for lipolysis?

a.why: Glucagon (and epinephrine) → protein kinase A phosphorylates and activates hormone-sensitive lipase. Insulin inhibits it.

stem: Ketogenesis is required when glucose is low to replenish which intermediate?

a.why: Massive beta-oxidation makes acetyl-CoA faster than the TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle can use it without oxaloacetate; ketogenesis combines acetyl-CoAs into acetoacetate, freeing coenzyme A.

stem: Depletion of which TCA cycle intermediate occurs after depletion of gluconeogenic substrates?

a.why: Gluconeogenesis drains oxaloacetate (to phosphoenolpyruvate). Once gluconeogenic substrates run out, oxaloacetate can't be replenished, so the TCA cycle stalls.

stem: What mechanism is activated during starvation after depletion of gluconeogenic substrates?

a.why: When gluconeogenic substrates (mainly muscle protein) run out in starvation, oxaloacetate drops, acetyl-CoA can't enter the TCA cycle, and the liver shifts to ketogenesis; ketones rise strongly.

stem: Which DNA base pair has the most binding energy?

a.why: Guanine–cytosine pairs form three hydrogen bonds versus two for adenine–thymine, so they have more binding energy. A–C and G–T are mismatches.

stem: When using PCR as a diagnostic test, which component comes from the patient?

a.why: In diagnostic polymerase chain reaction (PCR) the template DNA comes from the patient sample. Primers, nucleotides, Taq polymerase, and reverse transcriptase are supplied reagents.

stem: Which protein copies short strands of RNA during DNA replication to allow DNA polymerase to start?

a.why: DNA primase lays down short RNA primers so DNA polymerase has a 3' end to extend. Helicase unwinds; ligase seals nicks; topoisomerase relieves supercoiling.
a.flag: Stem says primase 'copies' RNA — it synthesizes RNA primers. Marked multi but one answer.

stem: Which enzyme allows the PCR reaction to be run with RNA?

a.why: Reverse transcriptase converts RNA into complementary DNA (cDNA) that PCR can then amplify (RT-PCR). Taq polymerase only copies DNA.
a.flag: Marked multi-select, but only one option fits.

stem: Some tumors may upregulate oncogenic miRNAs such as miR-9. What diagnostic test could be used to identify miR-9 in a sample?

a.why: Micro-RNA (miR-9) is RNA, so it must be reverse-transcribed before amplification: reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Plain PCR needs DNA; antibody tests detect proteins.

stem: Which type of translational regulation can cause the production of slightly different proteins from the same gene?

a.why: Differential (alternative) splicing joins different exon combinations, producing slightly different protein isoforms from one gene. The others change how much is made, not which version.
a.flag: Splicing is post-transcriptional; 'translational' is loose wording.

stem: Which diagnostic method uses an enzyme to multiply the signal, leading to increased sensitivity, but potentially increased false positives?

a.why: ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) links an enzyme to the antibody/antigen so a little enzyme makes lots of color: more sensitive than Coggins agglutination but more false positives (confirm with Coggins).
a.flag: PCR also uses an enzyme to amplify, but slide 24 uses this exact wording for ELISA. Marked multi.

stem: Which diagnostic test uses an antigen to determine if a sample has antibodies that can precipitate the antigen?

a.why: Agglutination: a known antigen probes serum for antibodies that clump and precipitate it (e.g., Brucella tube agglutination, Coggins test).

stem: Which level of protein structure is primarily driven by side chain interactions between distant parts of the peptide, especially hydrophobic interactions?

a.why: Tertiary structure = global collapse of one chain into its 3D shape, driven by side-chain interactions between distant residues, especially hydrophobic, often stabilized by disulfide bonds. Secondary = backbone hydrogen bonds.
a.flag: Marked multi-select, but only one option is correct.

stem: An allosteric site in an enzyme is described as the site where:
opts: Enzyme activity can be controlled away from the active site
The enzyme is linked to the cytoskeleton
The reactants bind and are converted to products

a.why: Allosteric site: where regulators bind away from the active site to control activity. Reactant binding/conversion is the active site; proteolytic activation is zymogen cleavage.
a.flag: Marked multi-select, but only one option is correct.

stem: Which of the following quantities predicts which direction a reaction will proceed?

a.why: ΔG (Gibbs free energy change) predicts direction: negative = forward. Activation energy (Ea) sets speed; KM (Michaelis constant) and Vmax (maximum velocity) are kinetics.

stem: Which class of enzymes are often produced as zymogens to prevent dangerous activation of their activity?

a.why: Proteases (e.g., trypsinogen → trypsin) are made as inactive zymogens and cleaved to activate, preventing self-digestion.

stem: Which enzyme is the main regulatory point for glycolysis?

a.why: Phosphofructokinase (PFK1) is the main regulatory point of glycolysis, activated by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate. Pyruvate kinase is co-regulated but secondary.

stem: Which of the following glucose transporters can push glucose up its concentration gradient?

a.why: Sodium-glucose linked transporter 1 (SGLT1) is secondary active, using the sodium gradient to move glucose uphill. GLUT (glucose transporter) 1, 2, 4 are passive.

stem: What is the purpose of lactic acid metabolism?

a.why: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) so glycolysis step 6 can keep making ATP without oxygen. It does not increase ATP per glucose.

stem: What intermediate builds up in the mitochondria during ischemia?

a.why: During ischemia, the TCA cycle runs forward from alpha-ketoglutarate and backward from oxaloacetate, both ending in succinate, which accumulates. Lactic acid builds in the cytosol, not mitochondria.

stem: When NADH is oxidized to NAD+ in complex I of the electron transport system, where does the energy from that oxidation go?
opts: The energy is lost as heat
The energy is stored in reduced coenzyme Q (QH2)
The energy is stored in a proton gradient

a.why: Complex I uses the energy released as electrons step down to pump about 4 protons into the intermembrane space, storing it in the proton gradient instead of losing it as heat.
a.flag: Electrons (some energy) also pass to reduced coenzyme Q (QH2); lecture frames the captured energy as the proton gradient.

stem: Why are the first three steps in the TCA cycle O2 dependent?
opts: Production of two molecules of CO2 requires O2
The final step in the cycle produces NADH and has a +ΔG
The first step in the cycle produces NADH
The third step in the cycle requires O2 as a reactant

a.why: Step 8 (malate → oxaloacetate) makes NADH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) with positive ΔG (free energy change); it needs O2 to regenerate NAD+. No O2 → no oxaloacetate → steps 1–3 stall.

stem: Why is glycogen stored instead of glucose?
opts: Glucose cannot be converted into fatty acids, glycogen can
Glucose is an osmolyte while glycogen is not
Glycogen can be mobilized much more rapidly than glucose
Glycogen has a higher energy density than glucose

a.why: Glucose is an osmolyte — storing lots of it would pull water into the cell. Glycogen is insoluble, so it doesn't raise osmotic pressure. Glucose is actually mobilized faster, not slower.

stem: Which of the following CANNOT be used for gluconeogenesis?

a.why: Palmitate (even-chain fatty acid) yields only acetyl-CoA, whose two carbons are lost as CO2 in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle — no net oxaloacetate. Alanine, glycerol, lactate, propionate are all gluconeogenic.

stem: Which hormones tend to increase gluconeogenesis in the liver? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Glucagon and epinephrine both activate protein kinase A (PKA) in liver, switching on gluconeogenesis. Insulin opposes it. Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) and somatostatin don't drive it; cortisol (not listed) would.

stem: Fructose 2,6 bisphosphate (F2,6BP) concentration in the cell is controlled by phosphofructokinase 2/fructose bisphosphatase 2 (PFK2/FBP2). Which of the following situations will tend to increase [F2,6BP] in the cell?
opts: Activation of AMP Kinase by increase [AMP] in the cell
Activation of PKA by increased [cAMP] due to the G s-coupled epinephrine receptor
Activation of PKA by increased [cAMP] due to the G s-coupled glucagon receptor
Activation of Protein Phosphatase 1 due to insulin signaling

a.why: Insulin → protein phosphatase 1 dephosphorylates PFK2/FBP2 (phosphofructokinase-2/fructose-bisphosphatase-2) → kinase side on → F2,6BP (fructose-2,6-bisphosphate) rises. Glucagon/epinephrine → PKA (protein kinase A) phosphorylation → phosphatase side → F2,6BP falls.
a.flag: Option a (AMP-activated kinase): in liver, AMPK isn't the taught regulator of PFK2; in heart, AMPK actually raises F2,6BP. Course answer is d.

stem: Which of the following amino acids CANNOT be glucogenic? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Leucine and lysine are the only strictly ketogenic amino acids. Isoleucine and tyrosine are both glucogenic and ketogenic, so they CAN be glucogenic.

stem: Why are ketogenic amino acids ketogenic?
opts: The aromatic rings cannot be converted to glucose
They can only form intermediates in the TCA cycle
They can only form products that are fully oxidized in the TCA cycle

a.why: They form only acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate. Acetyl-CoA's two carbons are fully oxidized to CO2 in the TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle, so no net carbon reaches oxaloacetate for glucose. 'Only TCA intermediates' would make them glucogenic.

stem: Which of the following molecules is a potent stimulator of carbamoyl phosphate synthase?

a.why: N-acetylglutamate is the obligate allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the first urea-cycle step. Glutamate is its precursor, not the activator.

stem: Which signals tend to increase the activity of Hormone Sensitive Lipase? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Hormone-sensitive lipase is active when phosphorylated: AMP (via AMP-activated protein kinase), epinephrine and glucagon (via protein kinase A). Citrate is a high-energy signal that drives lipogenesis; insulin dephosphorylates/inhibits it.
a.cite: LC20 slides 8 and regulation slide; LC20b transcript

stem: What is the proximal cause of the depletion of free coenzyme A that leads to ketogenesis?
opts: Depletion of exogenous glucose from the diet

a.why: Gluconeogenesis drains oxaloacetate; once gluconeogenic substrates run out, oxaloacetate can't be replenished, the TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle stalls, acetyl-CoA piles up and free coenzyme A disappears → ketogenesis.

stem: What functions are served by ketogenesis? (select ALL that apply)
opts: Providing a secondary energy source to the brain
Signaling the body on available energy levels

a.why: Ketogenesis regenerates free coenzyme A and supplies ketone bodies as fuel to brain and heart. Signaling energy levels isn't a taught function.
a.flag: Option d: acetoacetate → β-hydroxybutyrate does regenerate NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) in liver, but slides list only coenzyme A and fuel as functions.

stem: Which enzyme is the main control point for lipogenesis?

a.why: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is the committed, rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis (lipogenesis). Hormone-sensitive lipase is the control point for lipolysis — the paired trap.

stem: What mechanism is activated after a meal to maintain glucose homeostasis when exogenous glucose uptake starts to drop?

a.why: Post-meal into early fasting: dietary glucose falls, moderate glucagon triggers liver glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) as the main blood-glucose source. Gluconeogenesis takes over later, once glycogen runs out (late fasting).

stem: What process is strongly upregulated during starvation?

a.why: Starvation = gluconeogenic substrates exhausted; gluconeogenesis falls off and ketone bodies rise dramatically — ketosis is the hallmark of starvation.

stem: High levels of gluconeogenesis and very high levels of glucagon suggest what metabolic state?

a.why: Late fasting: glycogen gone, gluconeogenesis is the main glucose source, and glucagon is at its highest. In starvation glucagon exhausts and gluconeogenesis falls as substrates run out.

stem: During the early fasting state, what enzyme will be strongly upregulated in liver cells?

a.why: Early fasting: moderate glucagon → protein kinase A phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase; liver glycogen breakdown is the main glucose source. PFK-1 (phosphofructokinase-1) and PFK-2 kinase activity go down.

stem: Which DNA base pair has the most binding energy?

a.why: Guanine–cytosine pairs form three hydrogen bonds (adenine–thymine form two), so GC pairs hold the most binding energy. AC and GT are mismatches.

stem: How does the recognition step happen in DNA replication?
opts: A DNA polymerase coenzyme recruits the correct dNTP
DNA polymerase actively recruits the correct dNTP
dNTPs enter by simple diffusion and selection happens by hydrogen bonding

a.why: Deoxynucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) diffuse into the polymerase active site; the correct one is selected by complementary hydrogen bonding with the template base. No coenzyme or active recruitment.

stem: Which component of the PCR reaction makes DNA Primase unnecessary for PCR?

a.why: DNA primase normally lays down an RNA primer; in PCR (polymerase chain reaction) synthetic DNA primers are added, so Taq polymerase has a 3' end to extend.

stem: Which of the following is true about the 5’ cap on mRNA? (select ALL that apply)
opts: It is a signal for transcription factor binding
It is composed of a polyadenosine sequence
It slows degradation of the mRNA
It targets mRNA to the ribosome

a.why: The 5' cap (7-methylguanosine) protects mRNA from degradation and is recognized for ribosome binding/translation initiation. The poly-A tail is the polyadenosine part; transcription factors bind DNA, not the cap.

stem: Which enzyme allows the PCR reaction to be run with RNA?

a.why: Reverse transcriptase makes complementary DNA (cDNA) from RNA, which PCR (polymerase chain reaction) can then amplify (RT-PCR). Taq only copies DNA.
a.flag: Marked select-all but only one answer fits.

stem: The glucocorticoid receptor is an example of:

a.why: The glucocorticoid receptor binds specific DNA response elements to turn particular genes up or down — a regulatory (specific) transcription factor, not a general one (like TFIID/TFIIA) or a DNA-packing factor.

stem: Which of the following types of RNA carries the code for a protein?

a.why: Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries the protein-coding sequence. Transfer RNA brings amino acids, ribosomal RNA is ribosome structure, micro RNA regulates.

stem: Which protein can be activated/deactivated to globally regulate protein production?

a.why: eIF2 (eukaryotic initiation factor 2) phosphorylation shuts down translation initiation globally (e.g., stress response). DICER and iron-responsive-element binding protein act on specific RNAs; TFIIA is transcription.
a.flag: Marked select-all; only one answer fits.

stem: Which of the following types of RNA acts as a regulatory factor using cellular defense mechanisms against dsRNA?

a.why: Micro RNA (miRNA) forms double-stranded hairpins processed by DICER and uses the RNA-interference machinery (an antiviral defense against double-stranded RNA) to silence target mRNAs.

stem: Which of the following amino acids usually caries a negative charge at pH 7.4?

a.why: Glutamic acid's side-chain carboxyl (pKa ~4) is deprotonated at pH 7.4 → negative. Arginine is positive; asparagine and methionine are uncharged.
a.cite: LC14 slides (amino acid side chains); LC08 pH/pKa
a.flag: Marked select-all but only one answer fits.

stem: Which level of protein organization is driven by local interactions between the peptide backbone?

a.why: Secondary structure (alpha helix, beta sheet) is locally stable folding driven by hydrogen bonds along the peptide backbone. Tertiary = side-chain interactions.

stem: Which of the following diagnostic tests uses antibodies to probe a tissue slide?

a.why: Immunohistochemistry applies labeled antibodies to a tissue section to localize an antigen. ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) and agglutination use serum/fluids in wells or tubes; PCR (polymerase chain reaction) detects nucleic acid.

stem: A signal peptide on the N-terminus of a peptide will cause the protein to be expressed:

a.why: A signal peptide routes the protein into the rough endoplasmic reticulum → Golgi → secretory vesicles, a path continuous with the outside: default is secretion. Transmembrane orientation needs extra stop-transfer sequences; no signal = cytoplasm.

stem: Which of the following could cause a conformational change in a protein? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Anything forming or breaking an interaction — redox (disulfides), pH (charge), ion binding, ligand binding, phosphorylation — transmits force through the backbone and can change conformation.

stem: A mutation in the glucocorticoid receptor that removes the ubiquitination target would likely lead to:

a.why: Without the ubiquitin tag, the glucocorticoid receptor isn't degraded by the proteasome, so receptor accumulates and keeps driving immunosuppressive gene transcription → immunosuppression, not inflammation.

stem: Which of the following quantities predicts which direction a reaction will proceed?

a.why: ΔG (free energy change) predicts direction: negative = runs forward. Ea (activation energy) sets speed. Km and Vmax describe enzyme kinetics.

stem: Which of the following quantities predicts how quickly a reaction will proceed?

a.why: Per the course objective: Ea (activation energy) predicts how quickly a reaction runs; catalysts speed reactions by lowering Ea. ΔG gives direction only. Vmax is the tempting distractor.
a.flag: Vmax is a rate too, but it's enzyme-specific maximum; the course pairs speed with Ea.

stem: Which of the following quantities describes the substrate concentration at which an enzyme will catalyze the reaction at 50% of maximal velocity?

a.why: Km (Michaelis constant) = substrate concentration at half of maximal velocity. Low Km = high affinity.

stem: Which of the following glucose transporters can push glucose up its concentration gradient?

a.why: SGLT1 (sodium-glucose linked transporter 1) is secondary active, using the sodium gradient to move glucose up its concentration gradient. GLUT (glucose transporter) 1, 2, 4 are passive.

stem: Which molecule is an important allosteric feedforward regulator of Pyruvate Kinase?

a.why: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, made by the upstream phosphofructokinase-1 step, feed-forward activates pyruvate kinase so the lower glycolysis keeps pace.
a.cite: Outside course materials (standard biochemistry); LC16 regulation slide 14
a.flag: Slides don't name the pyruvate kinase activator explicitly; confirm before carding.

stem: Which of the following are potential products of the hexose monophosphate shunt? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: The hexose monophosphate (pentose phosphate) shunt makes NADPH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) and ribose-5-phosphate; the non-oxidative branch returns fructose-6-phosphate (and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate). No FADH2.
a.cite: Outside course materials (not in this year's slides)
a.flag: Pentose phosphate pathway not found in LC14–LC23 slides this year.

stem: Which of the following is the aerobic product of pyruvate?

a.why: With oxygen, pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA for the TCA (tricarboxylic acid) cycle. Lactate is the anaerobic product; acetate/propionate are microbial fermentation products.

stem: What is the purpose of lactic acid metabolism?

a.why: Lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate → lactate to regenerate NAD+ (oxidized nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) so glycolysis can keep running without oxygen. It produces no extra ATP.

stem: Which of the following anaerobic metabolic products of pyruvate are a significant source of nutrition for ruminants? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Rumen microbes ferment to volatile fatty acids — mainly acetate and propionate (plus butyrate) — absorbed as the cow's main energy. Acetyl-CoA is intracellular; ethanol isn't a major ruminant nutrient.

stem: Which molecule in the TCA cycle builds up during ischemia?

a.why: In ischemia NADH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) rises and succinate builds up (reverse running from fumarate); on reperfusion it's rapidly oxidized, driving reactive oxygen species.

stem: Step 1 in the TCA Cycle (oxaloacetate + acetyl-coA → citric acid), has a:

a.why: Step 1 (citrate synthase) has a very negative ΔG (free energy change); coupling it pulls the unfavorable step 8 (malate → oxaloacetate) forward.

stem: Why are the first three steps in the TCA cycle O2 dependent?
opts: Production of two molecules of CO2 requires O2
The final step in the cycle produces NADH and has a +ΔG
The first step in the cycle produces NADH
The third step in the cycle requires O2 as a reactant

a.why: Step 8 (malate → oxaloacetate) makes NADH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) with positive ΔG (free energy change); it needs O2 to regenerate NAD+. No O2 → no oxaloacetate → steps 1–3 stall.

stem: Which of the following are the relatively reduced forms? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Reduced forms carry the extra electrons/hydrogens: coenzyme QH2 (ubiquinol) and cytochrome c with Fe2+. Coenzyme Q and Fe3+ cytochrome c are oxidized.

stem: Which of the ETS complexes does NOT pump protons across the mitochondrial membrane?

a.why: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) passes electrons from FADH2 to coenzyme Q without pumping protons — why FADH2 yields ~1.5 ATP vs ~2.5 for NADH. Complexes I, III, IV pump.

stem: Compounds that complex with Fe3+ are likely to inhibit:

a.why: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) reduces O2 at a heme iron/copper center; cyanide and azide bind its ferric (Fe3+) heme a3 and block respiration.
a.flag: ETC inhibitors not found in this year's LC17 slides; complex III also has iron centers — confirm before carding.

stem: Why is glycogen stored instead of glucose?
opts: Glucose cannot be converted into fatty acids, glycogen can
Glucose is an osmolyte while glycogen is not
Glycogen can be mobilized much more rapidly than glucose
Glycogen has a higher energy density than glucose

a.why: Glucose is an osmolyte — storing lots of it would pull water into the cell. Glycogen is insoluble, so it doesn't raise osmotic pressure. Glucose is actually mobilized faster, not slower.

stem: Which enzyme is the main regulatory point for glycogen synthesis?

a.why: Glycogen synthase is the regulated step: active when dephosphorylated (insulin), feed-forward activated by glucose-6-phosphate. Branching enzyme and hexokinase aren't the control point.

stem: Which enzyme is deficient in glycogen storage disease type IIIa?

a.why: Glycogen storage disease type IIIa = deficiency of glycogen debranching enzyme (seen in curly-coated retrievers) — abnormal short-branched glycogen accumulates in liver and muscle.

stem: Which of the following CANNOT be used for gluconeogenesis?

a.why: Palmitate (even-chain fatty acid) yields only acetyl-CoA, whose two carbons are lost as CO2 in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle — no net oxaloacetate. Alanine, glycerol, lactate, propionate are all gluconeogenic.

stem: To bypass Pyruvate Kinase which is irreversible, pyruvate is converted to _________ in gluconeogenesis.

a.why: Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate → oxaloacetate in mitochondria; PEP carboxykinase (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase) then makes phosphoenolpyruvate, bypassing pyruvate kinase. Acetyl-CoA can't go back to glucose.

stem: Which hormone(s) tend to increase gluconeogenesis in the liver? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Epinephrine and glucagon activate protein kinase A in liver, turning gluconeogenesis on. Insulin inhibits it; somatostatin suppresses both insulin and glucagon secretion.

stem: Describe how an ELISA works. Why are ELISA tests very sensitive but prone to false positives?

a.why: Model answer: Antigen is fixed to a well; patient serum is added; antibodies to the antigen bind; a secondary antibody linked to an enzyme binds those; substrate is added and the enzyme makes a color. One enzyme turns over many substrate molecules, amplifying signal → very sensitive; color intensity/titer estimates concentration. That amplification also magnifies weak nonspecific or cross-reactive binding → false positives, so positives are confirmed (e.g., Coggins test, Western blot).

stem: Explain why there are two enzymes (glucokinase, hexokinase) that catalyze the phosphorylation of glucose.

a.why: Model answer: Hexokinase — low Km (Michaelis constant, <1 mM, high affinity), constitutive, in most tissues incl. brain, inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate; keeps glucose trapped even at low blood glucose. Glucokinase — high Km (~15 mM), inducible, liver and pancreatic beta cells, not inhibited by product; activity climbs with postprandial glucose (+58% from 4→7.5 mM vs 1.7% for hexokinase), so liver stores excess glucose and beta cells sense glucose to release insulin.

stem: Which of the following amino acids are only ketogenic? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Leucine and lysine are the only strictly ketogenic amino acids. Phenylalanine is both glucogenic and ketogenic; alanine and glutamate are glucogenic.

stem: Why are ketogenic amino acids ketogenenic?
opts: The aromatic rings cannot be converted to glucose
They can only form intermediates in the TCA cycle
They can only form products that are fully oxidized in the TCA cycle

a.why: They only form acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA)/acetoacetate, which the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle burns completely to carbon dioxide (CO2) — no net oxaloacetate, so no glucose.
a.flag: Wording 'fully oxidized' = acetyl-CoA carbons leave as CO2; options a–c are distractors.

stem: What are the purposes of ketogenesis? (select ALL that apply)
opts: To provide a secondary energy source to the brain
To signal the body on available energy levels

a.why: Ketogenesis regenerates free coenzyme A (CoA) when the TCA cycle stalls, and ketone bodies are an alternate brain fuel. Not taught as an energy signal; it does not regenerate oxidized nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+).
a.flag: Option b (signaling) not covered in lecture; treated as false.

stem: Why is ammonia toxic? (select ALL that apply)
opts: Ammonia is a base and can induce alkalosis
Ammonium is a cation that dysregulates K+ channels
Ammonia is an ionophore that disrupts the transmembrane potential
Ammonium is a signaling molecule that dysregulates cell cycle

a.why: Ammonia is a weak base (alkalosis), and ammonium (NH4+) is the same size/charge as potassium (K+), disrupting K+ channels in neurons. Third lecture mechanism (excess glutamine) isn't listed.

stem: How is an increase in ammonia concentration due to amino acid catabolism sensed in the liver cell?
opts: An increase in aspartate which activates Arginosuccinate Synthetase
An increase in N-acetylglutamate which activates Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthase
An increase in nitric oxide which activates Arginase
An increase in pH which activates Alkali Kinase

a.why: Amino acid catabolism raises liver glutamate and acetyl-CoA, which form N-acetylglutamate, activating carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I — the only urea cycle enzyme you need to know.

stem: How is creatine used by muscle cells?
opts: To buffer ammonium concentration changes caused by metabolism
To buffer pH changes caused by metabolism
To store high energy phosphate bonds
To serve as a relatively less toxic nitrogen waste

a.why: Muscle uses creatine to store high-energy phosphate bonds (phosphocreatine) for quick ATP regeneration. It is made from urea-cycle nitrogen, but its muscle job is energy storage.

stem: Which of the following ammonium wastes is least toxic and most concentrated in biological systems?

a.why: Uric acid (birds, reptiles) is least toxic and can be excreted highly concentrated as a near-insoluble paste. Urea is the mammalian answer for 'less toxic than ammonia', but uric acid beats it.
a.flag: Uric acid not found in this year's LC19 slides/transcript; standard comparative physiology.

stem: What is the main regulatory point for lipogenesis?

a.why: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is the committed, rate-limiting regulated step of fatty acid synthesis. Hormone-sensitive lipase controls lipolysis, not lipogenesis.

stem: Which of the following signals will upregulate hormone sensitive lipase in liver? (select ALL that apply)

a.why: Adenosine monophosphate (AMP, via AMP-activated kinase), epinephrine and glucagon (via protein kinase A) phosphorylate and activate hormone-sensitive lipase. Insulin and citrate favor lipogenesis.
a.flag: Hormone-sensitive lipase is classically adipose, not liver; lecture states AMP-activated kinase 'activates lipolysis' — AMP inclusion is from transcript framing.

stem: What is the proximal cause of the depletion of free coenzyme A that leads to ketogenesis?
opts: Depletion of exogenous glucose from the diet

a.why: When gluconeogenic substrates run out, gluconeogenesis drains oxaloacetate, the TCA cycle stalls, acetyl-CoA piles up and free coenzyme A disappears — triggering ketogenesis.

stem: Which of the following vitamins is a water-soluble antioxidant and important for collagen development?

a.why: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is water-soluble, an antioxidant, and a cofactor for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation in collagen. Vitamin E is the fat-soluble antioxidant.
a.flag: Vitamins not in this year's Exam 3 lectures.

stem: Which of the following vitamins is important for clotting factor maturation?

a.why: Vitamin K is needed to gamma-carboxylate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X so they can bind calcium and mature.
a.flag: Vitamins not in this year's Exam 3 lectures.

stem: What metabolic parameter separates the fed state from the early fasting state?
opts: Depletion of exogenous glucose from the diet

a.why: Fed (postprandial) to early fasting = running out of glucose absorbed from the diet; glycogenolysis then takes over.

stem: What metabolic parameter separates the late fasting state from the starvation state?
opts: Depletion of exogenous glucose from the diet

a.why: Late fasting to starvation = running out of gluconeogenic substrates. (Early to late fasting = glycogen depletion.) Ketones then rise sharply.

stem: In which metabolic state would glucagon signaling be highest?

a.why: Glucagon peaks in late fasting. In starvation it has been high so long it exhausts and begins to fall.

stem: Explain why uncontrolled diabetes mellitus can lead to ketoacidosis. Please refer to relevant hormones in your answer.

a.why: Model answer: No insulin (or insulin resistance) means cells act starved despite high blood glucose. Glucagon/epinephrine dominate: protein kinase A activates hormone-sensitive lipase (fatty acids flood liver) and drives gluconeogenesis, consuming oxaloacetate. TCA cycle stalls, acetyl-CoA accumulates, free coenzyme A falls, so liver makes ketone bodies (which it can't use — lacks 3-oxoacid CoA transferase). Production overwhelms kidney reabsorption/buffering: ketonuria, then ketoacidosis (>1.5 millimolar).

stem: The complementary nature of DNA strands is primarily conferred by:

a.why: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (adenine–thymine 2, guanine–cytosine 3) confer complementarity; covalent bonds form the backbone.

stem: Most differentiated cells in mature animals have minimal replicative ability and tumors often have mutations that allow unlimited replication (immortality). A mutation that causes over expression of which of the following proteins may help confer cellular immortality?

a.why: Telomerase extends chromosome ends (telomeres), preventing shortening-induced senescence — the key immortality enzyme in tumors. Polymerase, primase and helicase don't solve end shortening.

stem: When using PCR as a diagnostic test, which component comes from the patient?

a.why: The patient supplies the template deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA). Primers, nucleotides and Taq polymerase come in the kit; primers give specificity.

stem: Which portion of a gene recruits general transcription factors to mark the start of a gene?

a.why: Promoters recruit general transcription factors and ribonucleic acid (RNA) polymerase to the gene start. Enhancers bind specific/conditional factors to boost transcription.

stem: What modification is added to the 3’ end of mRNA to slow degradation?

a.why: The poly-adenosine (poly-A) tail on the 3-prime end slows messenger RNA (mRNA) degradation. The 7-methylguanosine cap is on the 5-prime end.

stem: Which enzyme allows PCR reactions to be run on RNA samples?

a.why: Reverse transcriptase copies RNA into complementary DNA (cDNA) so the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) can amplify it (RT-PCR).

stem: Which transcriptional regulation pathway tends to increase the amount of heterochromatin in a cell?
opts: Activation of conditional transcription factors (e.g. cortisol)
Activation of general transcription factors (e.g. TFIIB)

a.why: Methylation (DNA CpG and certain histone methylation) condenses chromatin into silent heterochromatin. Histone acetylation opens chromatin (euchromatin).

stem: Which of the following types of RNA acts as an enzyme?

a.why: Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is a ribozyme — it catalyzes peptide bond formation in the ribosome.

stem: Which protein is required to initiate translation and can be regulated to turn transcription on/off in a cell?

a.why: Eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2) delivers initiator transfer RNA to start translation; phosphorylating it shuts translation off globally. TFIIB is a transcription factor.
a.flag: Stem says 'transcription on/off' — almost certainly a typo for translation.

stem: Some tumors may upregulate oncogenic miRNAs such as miR-9. What diagnostic test could be used to identify miR-9 in a sample?

a.why: MicroRNA (miR-9) is RNA, so it must be reverse transcribed first — reverse transcription PCR. Plain PCR needs DNA; ELISA/IHC/agglutination detect proteins/antibodies.

stem: Isoleucine is a _________ amino acid.

a.why: Isoleucine is a branched-chain, hydrophobic non-polar amino acid (like leucine and valine).

stem: Global collapse of a peptide is driven by side chain interactions (especially hydrophobic interactions), leading to a unique three dimensional structure. This is called what?

a.why: Tertiary structure = global folding of one peptide driven by side-chain (especially hydrophobic) interactions. Secondary = backbone hydrogen bonds; quaternary = multiple subunits.

stem: Which diagnostics method uses an enzyme to multiply the signal, leading to increased sensitivity, but potentially increased false positives?

a.why: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) uses an enzyme to amplify the color signal — more sensitive than Coggins agglutination but more false positives, so positives are confirmed.

stem: If a peptide has a signal sequence in the middle of the peptide, where will the protein end up being expressed?

a.why: An internal signal sequence acts as a signal-anchor: the protein is inserted into the membrane with the N-terminus in the cytoplasm and C-terminus outside (type II transmembrane).
a.flag: This year's LC15 lecturer said internal signal-sequence 'odd rules' are not required. Internal signal-anchors can insert either orientation; d is the classic textbook answer.

stem: Ubiquitin is a signal that causes proteins to be:

a.why: Ubiquitin tags proteins for degradation by the proteasome.

stem: What is the name for a protease that is synthesized in an inactive form and must be cleaved to be active?

a.why: A zymogen (proenzyme) is an inactive protease precursor activated by cleavage. Enhancer/promoter/transcription factor are gene-regulation terms.

stem: Which quantity describes the affinity of an enzyme for a substrate?

a.why: The Michaelis constant (Km) reflects substrate affinity: low Km = high affinity. Change in free energy (ΔG) = spontaneity; activation energy (Ea) = barrier height.

stem: An allosteric site in an enzyme is described as the site where:
opts: Enzyme activity can be controlled away from the active site
The enzyme is linked to the cytoskeleton
The reactants bind and are converted to products

a.why: Allosteric sites bind regulators away from the active site to activate or inhibit the enzyme. Option d describes the active site; c describes zymogen activation.

stem: Which of the following molecules is an important gluconeogenic substrate in ruminants?

a.why: Propionate (volatile fatty acid from rumen fermentation) enters as succinyl-CoA → oxaloacetate → glucose. Acetate and acetyl-CoA cannot give net glucose.

stem: Which of the following are examples of reducing a molecule:
opts: Losing a proton and an electron

a.why: Reduction = gaining electrons, which makes a molecule less positive. Losing a proton and electron (hydrogen) or gaining a bond to oxygen are oxidations.

stem: When NADH is oxidized to NAD+ in complex I of the electron transport system, where does the energy from that oxidation go?
opts: The energy is lost as heat
The energy is stored in reduced coenzyme Q (QH2)
The energy is stored in a proton gradient

a.why: Complex I uses the energy from oxidizing reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) to pump protons, storing it in the proton gradient. QH2 just carries the electrons on.
a.flag: Some energy does remain in reduced coenzyme Q (QH2), but the answer the course wants is the proton gradient.

stem: Why does the liver store glycogen instead of glucose?
opts: Glucose has a lower energy density than glycogen
Glucose is an osmolyte while glycogen is not
Glucose can be used for glycolysis while glycogen can not

a.why: Glucose is an osmolyte — storing it would draw water into cells. Insoluble glycogen doesn't add to osmolality. Glycogen is readily broken down for glycolysis, so c is false.

stem: Which enzyme has a high Km that allows liver and muscle to take up more glucose to store as glycogen when blood glucose is high?

a.why: Glucokinase (high Km, not product-inhibited) in liver keeps phosphorylating glucose when blood glucose is high, trapping it for glycogen storage. Hexokinase has a low Km.
a.flag: Glucokinase is a liver (and pancreatic beta-cell) enzyme; muscle uses hexokinase — stem's 'and muscle' is inaccurate.

stem: Which glycogenolysis enzyme allows liver but not muscle to export glucose to the blood?

a.why: Glucose-6-phosphatase (liver, kidney) removes the phosphate so free glucose can exit via glucose transporter 2. Muscle lacks it, so its glycogen glucose stays in muscle.

stem: Which of the following CANNOT be used in gluconeogenesis?

a.why: Palmitic acid (even-chain fatty acid) breaks down to acetyl-CoA, which gives no net glucose. Glycerol, lactate and propionate are gluconeogenic.

stem: Which compound is central to bypassing step 10 of glycolysis (phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate) in gluconeogenesis?

a.why: Pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate from pyruvate, then phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase converts oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate — bypassing irreversible pyruvate kinase.

stem: Explain how hexokinase and glucokinase differ. Why is this important for glucose uptake in different tissues?

a.why: Model answer: Hexokinase (most tissues incl. muscle, brain) has a low Km (high affinity) and is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, so tissues take what they need even at low blood glucose. Glucokinase (liver, beta cells) has a high Km and isn't product-inhibited, so it only works hard when blood glucose is high — the liver soaks up excess for glycogen/fat after meals and leaves glucose for the brain during fasting.

stem: Why can a deficiency in pyruvate kinase cause hemolytic anemia?

a.why: Model answer: Mature red blood cells have no mitochondria, so glycolysis is their only ATP source. Pyruvate kinase deficiency cuts glycolytic ATP; without ATP the sodium-potassium pump fails, cells lose shape/deformability and are destroyed (hemolysis) — a regenerative hemolytic anemia, not blood loss (e.g., Basenji, beagle).

stem: Why is lactic acid produced when there is reduced O2 availability in mammalian cells? What are two major pathways for eliminating lactic acid during intense exercise?

a.why: Model answer: Without oxygen, the electron transport system can't reoxidize NADH, so NAD+ runs out and glycolysis (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step) stops. Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+. Elimination: (1) Cori cycle — liver converts lactate to glucose by gluconeogenesis; (2) oxidative tissues (heart, oxidative muscle) convert lactate back to pyruvate and burn it in the TCA cycle.

stem: Explain why succinate builds up in cells during ischemia. Why is this build up dangerous? What type of damage can happen during reperfusion? What could be a potential treatment for reperfusion damage?

a.why: Model answer: Ischemia — no oxygen, NAD+ depleted; TCA steps 6–8 run backward (fumarate → succinate via complex II) and steps 4–5 forward, so succinate accumulates. On reperfusion, rapid succinate oxidation over-reduces coenzyme Q, pushing electrons backward through complex I (reverse electron transport) → superoxide burst → oxidative damage/cell death. Treatment: restore flow early, reperfuse slowly/controlled; antioxidants or succinate dehydrogenase inhibition (malonate — outside course).
a.flag: Course offered only 'reperfuse slowly'; malonate/antioxidants are outside materials.

stem: Explain how gluconeogenesis vs glycolysis is regulated. You should mention fructose-2,6- bisphosphate and relevant hormones. What would happen if an individual was insulin resistant?

a.why: Model answer: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activates phosphofructokinase-1 (glycolysis) and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (gluconeogenesis). Insulin → phosphatases dephosphorylate PFK2/FBP2 → kinase side → F2,6BP rises → glycolysis. Glucagon/epinephrine → protein kinase A phosphorylates PFK2/FBP2 → phosphatase side → F2,6BP falls → gluconeogenesis. Insulin resistance: liver keeps running gluconeogenesis and glucose output despite hyperglycemia → worsened hyperglycemia.

stem: Which of the following is an example of a branched chain amino acid?

a.why: Valine is a branched-chain amino acid (with leucine and isoleucine). Tyrosine is aromatic; asparagine and glutamine are polar.

stem: Which of the following classes of amino acids are not metabolized by the liver postprandially?

a.why: Liver lacks the enzymes for branched-chain amino acid catabolism, so they pass through to muscle. Aromatic amino acids are preferentially metabolized by liver.

stem: Which of the following molecules is a potent stimulator of carbamoyl phosphate synthase?

a.why: N-acetylglutamate (made from glutamate + acetyl-CoA during amino acid catabolism) is the potent activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. Glutamate is only its precursor.

stem: Which of the following is a spontaneous break down product of phosphocreatine?

a.why: Phosphocreatine spontaneously (non-enzymatically) cyclizes to creatinine, which kidneys excrete — why serum creatinine tracks kidney function and muscle mass.

stem: Which of the following situations does NOT stimulate Acetyl-CoA Carboxylase?

a.why: Epinephrine activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates and inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase. Citrate (feed-forward) and insulin (dephosphorylation) activate it; high ATP = high energy, low AMP-activated kinase.
a.flag: ATP is not a direct activator; it 'stimulates' only indirectly (low AMP → less AMP-activated kinase inhibition).

stem: Glucagon signaling stimulates which of the following enzymes?

a.why: Glucagon → protein kinase A → phosphorylates and activates hormone-sensitive lipase (lipolysis) while inhibiting acetyl-CoA carboxylase. Other options aren't real course enzymes/targets.

stem: Which of the following hormones inhibits protein breakdown and shifts the system to anabolism (protein synthesis)?

a.why: Insulin builds protein mainly by inhibiting protein breakdown, shifting toward anabolism. Glucagon and epinephrine are catabolic; thyroid-stimulating hormone is off-target.

stem: Ketone bodies are only produced in significant quantities during which phase of metabolism?

a.why: Starvation: gluconeogenic substrates run out, oxaloacetate is depleted, so acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) is shunted to ketone bodies. Late fasting makes only a little ketone — not yet significant.
a.flag: Late fasting has minor ketone production per lecture; 'significant' points to starvation.

stem: Please explain why amino acids that are metabolized into acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate cannot be glucogenic.

a.why: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible, so acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) can't go back to pyruvate. In the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, acetyl-CoA's 2 carbons enter but 2 carbons leave as carbon dioxide — no net oxaloacetate gain, so no net glucose. Acetoacetate breaks down to acetyl-CoA, same dead end.

stem: Please explain why and under what conditions ketogenesis occurs.

a.why: Occurs when oxaloacetate is depleted — late fasting/starvation, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, high-producing dairy cows. Low insulin/high glucagon drives fat breakdown; liver beta-oxidation floods acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA), but oxaloacetate is pulled into gluconeogenesis so acetyl-CoA can't enter the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. Liver converts it to ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate), exported as fuel for brain/muscle, sparing glucose and recycling coenzyme A.

stem: What is the liver's main purpose in energy metabolism? How does it accomplish this goal under different conditions (fed state, early fasting, late fasting, starvation, intense exercise)?

a.why: Main job: maintain blood glucose for other tissues. Fed: insulin → glycolysis, glycogen synthesis, fatty acid synthesis (exported as very-low-density lipoprotein). Early fasting: glucagon → glycogenolysis. Late fasting: glycogen gone → gluconeogenesis (amino acids, lactate, glycerol; propionate in ruminants), fatty acid oxidation, a little ketogenesis. Starvation: substrates run out → ketogenesis dominates. Intense exercise: epinephrine → glycogenolysis plus gluconeogenesis from muscle lactate (Cori cycle).

stem: When using PCR as a diagnostic test, which component confers selectivity on the reaction?

a.why: Primers bind only the target sequence, so they decide what gets amplified (selectivity). Template comes from the patient; nucleotides and polymerase are generic.

stem: General transcription factors bind to which part of a gene?

a.why: General transcription factors assemble on the promoter (e.g., TATA box) to recruit ribonucleic acid (RNA) polymerase II. Enhancers bind specific/regulatory transcription factors, not the general ones.

stem: Addition of a 3’ poly-adenosine cap to mRNAs:
opts: Is an intermediate in the splicing reaction
Allows binding of the mRNA to ribosomes

a.why: The 3' poly(A) tail protects messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) from exonuclease degradation (and aids export/translation). Ribosome binding is mainly the 5' cap's job.
a.flag: Stem says '3' poly-adenosine cap' — it's a tail, not a cap.

stem: Which of the following RNA types is NOT required for translation?

a.why: Micro ribonucleic acid (miRNA) regulates/silences messenger RNA; translation itself needs messenger RNA (template), ribosomal RNA (ribosome), and transfer RNA (amino acid delivery).

stem: Which of the following amino acids is hydrophobic?

a.why: Leucine has a nonpolar branched alkyl side chain. Aspartic acid (negative), lysine (positive), threonine (polar hydroxyl) are hydrophilic.

stem: What targets a protein to the proteasome for degradation?

a.why: Polyubiquitin chains tag proteins for proteasomal degradation. Phosphorylation/acetylation/methylation mainly change activity or interactions.

stem: What class of proteins are most often expressed as pro-enzyme zymogens?

a.why: Proteases (e.g., trypsinogen → trypsin) are made as inactive zymogens and activated by cleavage, so they don't digest the cell that makes them.

stem: Which quantity can predict whether a reaction will go in the forward or the reverse direction?

a.why: Gibbs free energy change (ΔG): negative = proceeds forward spontaneously, positive = reverse. Activation energy (Ea) sets rate only; Michaelis constant (Km) is substrate affinity.

stem: Which quantity does a catalyst reduce?

a.why: Catalysts lower activation energy (Ea) to speed the reaction; they do not change Gibbs free energy change (ΔG) or the equilibrium.

stem: Citrate binds to phosphofructokinase and changes the activity of the enzyme. This would be an example of:

a.why: Citrate binds phosphofructokinase-1 at a regulatory site (not active site) and inhibits it — allosteric regulation. Not feed-forward: citrate is downstream of phosphofructokinase (that would be feedback).
a.flag: Citrate→PFK-1 is technically feedback inhibition (allosteric). 'Feedforward' is wrong because citrate is downstream.

stem: Why is Pyruvate Dehydrogenase an aerobic enzyme?
opts: Because it uses O2 as a substrate
Because a previous step used O2 as a substrate

a.why: Pyruvate dehydrogenase uses no oxygen directly but makes NADH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide); regenerating NAD+ requires the oxygen-dependent electron transport system. Without oxygen NAD+ runs out.

stem: What is the main function of lactate metabolism?
opts: To generate ATP for cellular metabolism
To generate NADH for cellular metabolism
To regenerate NAD+ in the absence of oxygen
To regenerate FAD in the absence of oxygen

a.why: Lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactate, oxidizing NADH back to NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) so glycolysis can keep running without oxygen. Lactate itself yields no ATP.

stem: Which of the following is an important ruminant microbial anaerobic metabolite that can be used in gluconeogenesis?

a.why: Propionate (a volatile fatty acid) → propionyl-coenzyme A → succinyl-CoA → oxaloacetate → glucose. Acetate is not glucogenic (2-carbon, like acetyl-CoA).

stem: In this reaction: 2 Fe3+ + NADH → 2 Fe2+ + NAD+ + H+ which compound is reduced?

a.why: Fe3+ gains an electron to become Fe2+ — that's reduction. NADH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) is oxidized (the reducing agent); Fe2+ is the product, not the compound reduced.

stem: Which of the following electron transport system complexes is not a proton pump?

a.why: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) passes FADH2 (reduced flavin adenine dinucleotide) electrons to ubiquinone without pumping protons — why FADH2 yields ~1.5 ATP vs ~2.5 for NADH.

stem: What is the direct energy source for ATP synthase?

a.why: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthase is driven directly by protons flowing down their gradient (proton-motive force). Electron transport/NADH oxidation only build that gradient — indirect.

stem: Which of the following is NOT true about the importance of glycogen storage?
opts: Fatty acids cannot be converted into glucose
Fatty acids cannot be used anaerobically
Glycogen can be broken down very rapidly
Glycogen has a higher energy density than lipids
Glycogen is not an osmolyte while glucose is

a.why: False: glycogen is hydrated and less reduced, so lipids store far more energy per gram. The rest are true reasons glycogen matters (rapid mobilization, anaerobic use, no fat→glucose, low osmotic effect).

stem: Which tissue expresses Glucose-6-phosphatase?

a.why: Liver (and kidney) express glucose-6-phosphatase, so they can release free glucose into blood. Muscle lacks it — its glycogen serves only itself.

stem: Which compound is important in bypassing Pyruvate Kinase in gluconeogenesis?

a.why: Pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate from pyruvate; phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase turns oxaloacetate into phosphoenolpyruvate — bypassing irreversible pyruvate kinase.

stem: Which hormone activates glycolysis and glycogen synthesis and inhibits gluconeogenesis in the liver?

a.why: Insulin → protein phosphatases → active glycogen synthase, fructose-2,6-bisphosphate up (glycolysis on, gluconeogenesis off). Glucagon and epinephrine do the opposite via protein kinase A.

stem: FAS receptor can be expressed in two different forms: a membrane bound receptor that induces apoptosis and a soluble receptor that prevents apoptosis. Propose a regulatory mechanism that could be responsible for the expression of these two similar proteins. Explain your answer.

a.why: Alternative splicing of the same pre-messenger ribonucleic acid (pre-mRNA): including the exon encoding the transmembrane domain gives the membrane-bound receptor; skipping it gives a secreted soluble receptor. Same gene, similar sequence, different localization/function. (Alternatively, proteolytic cleavage/shedding of the extracellular domain.)

stem: ELISA is one of the diagnostic assays we discussed in class. What are some of the benefits of an ELISA? What are some of the drawbacks?

a.why: Benefits: sensitive, specific, quantitative, inexpensive, high-throughput, can detect antigen or antibody, no special equipment beyond plate reader. Drawbacks: antibody detection can't distinguish current infection vs past exposure/vaccination; cross-reactivity/false positives; needs good antibodies; antibodies lag behind infection (window period); multi-step, wash-dependent.

stem: Pyruvate Kinase regulation:
opts: What compound is an important allosteric activator of Pyruvate Kinase?
Why is the product of this enzyme an important regulator of Pyruvate Kinase?
If there is a loss of function mutation in Pyruvate Kinase that makes it insensitive to this compound, what tissue would you expect to be most affected (i.e. where would you see symptoms first)?

a.why: (a) Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. (b) Phosphofructokinase-1. (c) Feed-forward activation: when the committed step runs, pyruvate kinase is turned on to pull flux through to pyruvate and ATP, avoiding intermediate buildup. (d) Red blood cells — no mitochondria, entirely glycolysis-dependent for ATP → hemolytic anemia (pyruvate kinase deficiency).
a.cite: LC16 slides (Pyruvate Kinase Deficiency); standard biochemistry for (a)–(c)

stem: Why is reperfusion post ischemia often more destructive than the ischemia itself? Please describe (1) the type of damage that occurs; (2) what causes that damage; and (3) how oxaloacetate and succinate are central to this process. Propose a treatment to prevent or reduce reperfusion damage.

a.why: (1) Oxidative damage from reactive oxygen species (superoxide). (2) During ischemia, tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle steps 6–8 run backward (oxaloacetate → malate → fumarate → succinate) to regenerate NAD+, so succinate builds up. On reperfusion, complex II rapidly oxidizes succinate, over-reducing the quinone pool → reverse electron flow at complex I → superoxide burst. Treatment: reperfuse slowly/gradually; antioxidants or succinate dehydrogenase inhibitor (e.g., malonate — outside course).

stem: Why do milking cows on high fiber diets have a high risk of ketosis?

a.why: High fiber → rumen microbes make mostly acetate (not glucogenic) and less propionate (the main glucose precursor). Lactation drains huge glucose for lactose, so liver gluconeogenesis consumes oxaloacetate. Fat mobilization floods liver with acetyl-coenzyme A that can't enter the tricarboxylic acid cycle → ketone bodies.
a.cite: LC17-18 transcript (dairy cow case); LC18/LC20 slides

stem: Which of the following molecules is an important intermediate in amino acid transamination/ deamination reactions?

a.why: Aminotransferases move amino groups onto α-ketoglutarate making glutamate; glutamate dehydrogenase then deaminates it releasing ammonium. Glutamate is the central nitrogen collector.

stem: Which of the following classes of amino acids are preferentially catabolized by the liver after a meal?

a.why: Liver preferentially catabolizes aromatic amino acids; branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) bypass the liver and are catabolized in muscle.
a.flag: Marked multi-select, but only (a) is correct.

stem: Which of the following amino acids CANNOT be glucogenic?

a.why: Lysine (with leucine) is strictly ketogenic — degraded only to acetyl-coenzyme A/acetoacetate. Isoleucine is both glucogenic and ketogenic; alanine and aspartate are glucogenic.

stem: Which of the following molecules is an allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthase?

a.why: N-acetylglutamate is the required allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the urea cycle's rate-limiting step.
a.flag: Marked multi-select, but only (c) is correct.

stem: What function is creatine used for in the body?
opts: Signal to upregulate the urea cycle
Storage of ammonia in a non-toxic state
Storage of high energy phosphate bonds

a.why: Creatine phosphate (phosphocreatine) stores high-energy phosphate in muscle to quickly regenerate ATP. It's also an alternate nitrogen waste, but not ammonia storage.

stem: What marks the transition from the fed state to early fasting?

a.why: Fed → early fasting: meal fully absorbed, no more dietary (exogenous) glucose from intestine; liver switches to glycogenolysis.

stem: What marks the transition from the early fasting stage to the late fasting stage?

a.why: Early → late fasting: liver glycogen runs out; gluconeogenesis takes over.

stem: What marks the transition from the late fasting stage to starvation?

a.why: Late fasting → starvation: gluconeogenic substrates (mainly muscle protein) run out; gluconeogenesis falls and ketosis rises sharply.

stem: Please explain the regulation of lipid metabolism. In particular, please describe:
opts: What hormone is expressed when blood glucose is low? ________________________

Activity of which enzyme is upregulated by this hormone AND what pathway is activated by this enzyme? Activity of which enzyme is downregulated by this hormone AND what pathway is deactivated by this enzyme?

a.why: (a) Glucagon (epinephrine also). (b) Upregulated: hormone-sensitive lipase (phosphorylated by protein kinase A) → lipolysis/triglyceride breakdown, feeding fatty acid beta-oxidation. Downregulated: acetyl-coenzyme A carboxylase (inactivated by protein kinase A phosphorylation) → fatty acid synthesis off; falling malonyl-CoA also releases carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, letting beta-oxidation run.

stem: Please describe ketogenesis. In particular, please describe:
opts: Depletion of what intermediate leads to ketogenesis? ________________________
What causes the depletion of the intermediate from (a)?
When the intermediate in (a) is depleted, why is ketogenesis necessary?
Why can uncontrolled diabetes mellitus lead to ketoacidosis?

a.why: (a) Oxaloacetate. (b) Oxaloacetate is pulled out for gluconeogenesis during low glucose (fasting, starvation, lactation, diabetes). (c) Beta-oxidation keeps producing acetyl-coenzyme A that can't enter the tricarboxylic acid cycle; converting it to ketones frees coenzyme A and exports fuel to brain/muscle. (d) No insulin → unchecked lipolysis and gluconeogenesis despite high glucose → massive ketone production exceeding use; ketone acids exhaust buffering → acidosis.

stem: The complementary nature of DNA strands is primarily conferred by:

a.why: Base pairing (A–T, G–C) is via hydrogen bonds, which give complementarity. Covalent phosphodiester bonds form the backbone; hydrophobic stacking stabilizes but isn't specific.

stem: When using PCR as a diagnostic test, which component comes from the patient being tested?

a.why: The template deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is the patient's sample; primers, nucleotides and polymerase are supplied reagents.

stem: Which of the following parts of a gene is never found in the final mRNA?

a.why: Introns are spliced out of pre-messenger ribonucleic acid. Exons, start codon and stop codon remain in mature mRNA.

stem: What is found on the 5’ end of a mature mRNA?

a.why: The 5' cap is 7-methylguanosine (linked 5'-to-5' triphosphate). Polyadenosine is on the 3' end.

stem: Which of the following types of RNA acts as an enzyme?

a.why: Ribosomal ribonucleic acid (rRNA) is a ribozyme — it catalyzes peptide bond formation (peptidyl transferase) in the ribosome.

stem: Which part of the mRNA is necessary for binding to a ribosome? (select the best answer)

a.why: Ribosome (small subunit with initiation factors) recognizes the 5' cap and scans to the start codon. The start codon sets the reading frame but isn't the binding site; there's no '3' cap'.

stem: Lysine, at pH 7.4, is a:

a.why: Lysine's side-chain amine (pKa ~10.5) is protonated at pH 7.4 → positively charged (basic amino acid).

stem: Which of the following levels of structure is caused primarily by interactions between amino acid side chains within one peptide chain?

a.why: Tertiary structure = 3-dimensional folding from side-chain (R-group) interactions within one chain. Secondary = backbone hydrogen bonds; quaternary = between chains.

stem: Which of the following diagnostic assays tests for the ability of serum antibodies to precipitate an antigen?

a.why: Agglutination/precipitation assays rely on antibodies cross-linking antigen into visible clumps. ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) uses enzyme-linked detection, not precipitation.
a.flag: Agglutination strictly = particulate antigen clumping; precipitation = soluble antigen. Agglutination is still the only fitting option.

stem: If a protein is ubiquitinated, what is its likely disposition?

a.why: Ubiquitination (polyubiquitin) targets proteins to the proteasome for degradation.

stem: Acetylation of histones near a gene usually:
opts: Decreases the density of DNA packaging
Decreases the transcription of the gene
Increases the density of DNA packaging
Increases the transcription of the gene

a.why: Acetylation neutralizes lysine positive charges on histones, loosening their grip on DNA → less dense chromatin → more accessible → increased transcription.

stem: Which of the following events could change the conformation of a protein?

a.why: All four change conformation: ion binding, pH (alters side-chain charges), ligand binding (allosteric/induced fit), phosphorylation (adds negative charge).
a.flag: Not marked multi-select and no 'all of the above' option in source; all four are correct. Likely original had 'all of the above' or was select-all.

stem: Describe what you would expect to find after DNA replication if DNA ligase is non-functional.

a.why: Leading strand is fine, but lagging strand stays as unjoined Okazaki fragments — nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone remain after primer removal and gap fill, giving fragmented, unstable DNA (strand breaks, cell cycle arrest/death).

stem: You are studying T-cell activation and CD45, a transmembrane protein essential to T-cell activation. You are using an antibody to purify CD45 from T-cells before and after activation and then resolving the protein on an acrylamide gel to determine size and relative abundance. You notice that the CD45 purified before T-cell activation is significantly larger (220 kDa) than the CD45 purified after T-cell activation (180 kDa). What two regulatory processes discussed in class could explain this observation and how could you determine which of these processes was occurring?

a.why: (1) Alternative splicing — different exon combinations give 220 vs 180 kilodalton isoforms (true for CD45). (2) Post-translational modification — proteolytic cleavage or loss of glycosylation. Distinguish: reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) of CD45 messenger RNA before/after activation (different-sized transcripts = splicing); if mRNA is the same, test deglycosylation enzyme treatment or protease inhibitors/N-terminal antibodies.
